Decode Modeling

Decode Modeling

Author: Yue Lu
Date: November 2026

First-principles analytical derivation of decode-phase latency, throughput, and memory bandwidth for large language model (LLM) inference on a cluster. The chapters are intentionally implementation-independent — they describe the cost model, the assumptions, and the symbol conventions; the FLARE code in spiceMonkey/flare-llm is one possible realization.

Where to start. Decode and TPOT is the centerpiece: memory footprint, memory traffic, compute, communication, and the step time and throughput built from them. Three chapters cover the supporting physics it references:

  • Attention variants — multi-head, grouped-query, multi-query and latent attention, and what each costs per token per layer
  • Memory hierarchy — multi-tier roofline that generalizes the single-HBM model to SRAM-augmented devices
  • 3D-stacked DRAM bandwidth — memory bandwidth derived from the parameters of a hybrid-bonded interface

For the collective-communication cost model that decode references throughout (α–β cost form, ring / tree / hierarchical algorithms, topology composition, in-network reduction), see the dedicated tutorial at spicemonkey.github.io/collective-comm — linked from the Collective Communication chapter.

Serving and deployment. Four chapters build on the decode model: KV cache management (paged allocation, fragmentation, and how many sequences a device holds), Framework overhead (host-side latency per request, and the constants that describe each serving stack), SLO feasibility (which batch sizes and partitions meet latency targets), and Phase and memory disaggregation, which sizes separate prefill and decode pools, prices the cache transfer between them, and adds host memory for caches that are not being decoded.

Scope and companion documents. This book is intentionally focused on decode and on the serving questions that sit directly on top of it. Three derivations that the chapters cite are companion documents and are not chapters of this book: the prefill and time-to-first-token derivation, the end-to-end metrics derivation, and the suite’s combined notation reference. Where a chapter cites one of them, the citation is plain text and says that the document is outside the book; nothing a chapter needs in order to be read is left there — the sharding factors, the batch divisor and the replica size, for example, are defined in Decode and TPOT §1.4. Citations of the form collectives/NN_name.md refer to the chapters of the collective-communication tutorial linked above.

1. Memory Footprint

This section defines parameter sizes and memory footprint for a given set of model parameters. The memory footprint include those from model weights, per-token activation/working memories, and KV cache. We avoid model-wide parameter aggregation here and instead focus on per-layer quantities, because pipeline-parallel stages own disjoint sets of layers. All parameter definitions assume stored precision of b bytes per element (e.g., bf16 = 2 bytes). A serving stack may store the KV cache and the activations at a different width than the weights; where the distinction matters the text writes bkv​ for a cache element and bact​ for an activation, logit or message element, and both default to b.

Layout and mode parameterization. Per-device formulas in §1.4 and below (and analogously in §2.1 / §2.3 / §3.5 / §5.3 / §5.5) are written in terms of the per-component effective sharding factors Dattn​, Dexp​, Dkv​, Demb​, the batch divisor Dbatch​, and the collective group sizes GTP​, GEP​ rather than raw TP / EP divisors. All of them are defined in §1.4. This lets a single expression cover all four production-relevant combinations of layout and attention mode — orthogonal + TP-attention, orthogonal + DP-attention (DSv3 / SGLang on disjoint TP and EP groups), co-located + DP-attention (DSv3 / SGLang on a single NVLink island, max(TP,EP) GPUs per replica), and co-located + TP-attention (the DeepSeek-R1 deployment on one NVL72 rack: TP=EP overlaid on the same GPU set with attention head-sharded across that group) — without conditional branching. The lookup table in §1.4 maps the abstract factors to each of the four configurations; later sections cite it instead of repeating it.

1.0 Parameter Definitions (P vs W)

For any weight matrix W, the parameter count is

P(W)=number of elements in W

Total stored parameter memory is

Mθ​=P⋅b

1.1 Model Parameter Memory

Embedding and LM Head Parameters

Modern LLM architectures (GPT-3/4, LLaMA families, PaLM, Qwen, DeepSeek, etc.) typically use embedding dimension E=H, so all internal projections operate on vectors in RH.

For the token embedding:

Wemb​∈RV×H,Pemb​=VH

If the LM head is tied with embeddings, i.e. Wlm​=WembT​ so that Wemb​ can be re-used:

Plm​=0

If untied:

Wlm​∈RH×V,Plm​=VH

Attention Parameters

For hidden size H, head dimension dhead​, and KV dimension Hkv​=nkv​dhead​ (supporting grouped-query attention where nkv​≤nq​ [GQA] and multi-query attention where nkv​=1 [MQA]):

  • WQ​∈RH×H
  • WK​∈RH×Hkv​
  • WV​∈RH×Hkv​
  • WO​∈RH×H

In GQA, each of the nq​ query heads produces a dhead​-dimensional output; the concatenated result across all query heads is nq​×dhead​=H-dimensional, regardless of how many KV heads are used. The output projection therefore always maps RH→RH.

Parameter counts:

PQ​=H2,PK​=HHkv​,PV​=HHkv​,PO​=H2

We define attention parameters:

Pattn​=PQ​+PK​+PV​+PO​

Variant note. Models with non-MHA attention (Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), sliding-window attention, DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), hybrid linear / full attention) substitute a different Pattn​ formula here. Per-variant decompositions and worked examples are in attention.md (e.g. attention.md §3.3 for MLA’s six-matrix per-layer parameter sum). The decode.md outer composition (per-device sharding, multi-layer aggregation, traffic, FLOPs roll-up) is unchanged — only this term is replaced.

Unified FFN Parameters (Dense or MoE)

Each transformer layer contains an FFN module. In modern LLM architectures, this FFN is almost always implemented as a gated MLP (GeLU/SiLU/GLU/SwiGLU–style) with three linear projections:

  • a gate projection,
  • an “up” projection (expansion),
  • a “down” projection (contraction).

Convention: This document assumes gated FFN (SwiGLU/GeGLU style) throughout, giving three weight matrices per FFN block. Standard (non-gated) FFN uses two matrices (up + down), yielding 2HI parameters. The gated form is used by LLaMA, Qwen, DeepSeek, and most modern LLMs.

For a hidden size H and FFN intermediate dimension I, this yields an FFN parameter count

PFFN​=3HINexp​.

Here Nexp​ denotes the number of experts per layer:

  • For a dense MLP model: I=Idense​,Nexp​=1.
  • For a MoE model: I=Imoe​, with Nexp​>1.

These two model cases are mutually exclusive per layer.

LayerNorm parameters

LayerNorm or RMSNorm contain O(H) parameters (scale and optional bias). These are negligible compared to attention and FFN weights and are omitted in scaling formulas.

1.2 Activation Memory (Per-token Working Memory)

During autoregressive decoding, the model processes one token at a time. As a result, the only activations that need to be stored in memory are the temporary, layer-local working buffers used in the forward pass of the current token.

These activations are not reused across layers or across tokens and therefore are:

  • not dependent on sequence length S,
  • proportional to batch size B (each sequence in the batch needs its own working buffers),
  • not EP- or TP-sharded,
  • and extremely small relative to model parameter memory (Section 1.1) and KV cache memory (Section 1.3).

Below we account for all activation tensors in a model layer that must be alive concurrently for one decoding token.

Q, K, V projections

For the current hidden state h∈RH, the layer computes:

  • Q∈RH
  • K∈RHkv​
  • V∈RHkv​

This contributes:

H+2Hkv​

Attention score accumulation buffer (FlashAttention-like kernels)

Attention score computation normally requires a temporary buffer. FlashAttention-style fused kernels avoid storing full S-length score vectors and instead use a single internal workspace of size H during streaming softmax.

This adds:

+H

Attention output buffer

After applying attention weights to V and combining across heads, we form the attention output Oattn​∈RH.

This output must exist before the output projection is applied, contributing:

+H

FFN working buffer

Following attention and normalization, the FFN block needs at least one temporary buffer of size H to hold either the FFN input or the FFN output before residual addition. Even with kernel fusion, this buffer cannot always overlap with the attention intermediates.

This adds:

+H

Summing all simultaneously required buffers per sequence:

Pact​=4H+2Hkv​

In bytes, for a batch of B sequences: Mact,layer​=B⋅(4H+2Hkv​)⋅b

This footprint is small compared to parameter memory and KV cache, even at large batch sizes. For example, at B=128, H=8192, Hkv​=1024, b=2: Mact,layer​≈9 MB per layer — negligible against hundreds of GB of parameter memory.

1.3 KV Cache Memory

Section 1.1 described the memory footprint of model parameters (static), and Section 1.2 covered the activation memory required during decoding (per-token, dynamic). This section describes the KV cache, which is a runtime structure generated during the pre-fill phase, when the model processes the entire input sequence of length S.

During pre-fill, each attention layer produces:

  • one key vector of dimension Hkv​,
  • one value vector of dimension Hkv​,

for each input token. Because decoding adds only one new token at a time, the vast majority of KV memory comes from pre-fill, not decoding.

For a single attention layer, the KV cache consists of:

  • Keys: K∈RS×Hkv​
  • Values: V∈RS×Hkv​

The KV cache size scales with Hkv​=nkv​dhead​; using grouped-query attention (nkv​<nq​) [GQA] or multi-query attention (nkv​=1) [MQA] directly reduces this footprint.

Variant note. Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) further compresses the per-token KV cache by storing a head-shared latent of dimension dc​+dqk,rope​ instead of 2Hkv​. For DSv3-class numbers this is roughly 25× smaller than the dense MHA equivalent. See attention.md §3.4 for the MLA per-token-per-layer formula and attention.md §3.6 for sharding behavior under TP-attn / DP-attn.

Thus, the total KV elements for one layer are:

PKV,layer​=S⋅(2Hkv​)=2SHkv​

In bytes (per sequence):

MKV,layer​=2SHkv​⋅b(per sequence, per layer)

This is static once pre-fill is complete; decoding contributes only an additional 2Hkv​b per generated token, which is negligible relative to the full cache.

1.4 Per-device Memory Footprint After Parallelism Sharding

So far we’ve completed the all the memory footprint estimation for a model layer. When we introduce different parallelism schemes, some of these memories would be sharded by one or more of these parallelism dimensions, resulting in a somewhat complicated memory aggregateion per device. We now describe how these parameters are distributed across devices under PP/EP/TP/SP, and then derive simple modeling approximations.

Two deployment choices change how each component is sharded. The layout says whether the TP and EP groups are disjoint device sets (orthogonal: a replica is EP groups of TP devices) or the same devices (co-located: one group of max(TP,EP) devices, which requires TP=EP whenever both are greater than 1; with TP=1 or EP=1 there is nothing to overlay and the two layouts describe the same replica). The attention mode says whether attention is head-sharded across the TP group (TP-attention) or its weights are replicated on every rank and the batch is split across the ranks instead (DP-attention). To carry both through every per-device formula without branching, each shardable component gets a named effective divisor:

  • Dattn​ — divisor of the attention weights (Q/K/V/O projections) on one device.
  • Dexp​ — divisor of the FFN / expert weights on one device. Dense FFN always uses Dexp​=TP (no EP axis to overlap; co-location does not apply); MoE FFN follows the table.
  • Dkv​ — divisor of one sequence’s KV cache on one device, by head or by sequence, excluding SP. KV memory and traffic carry an additional /SP factor on top of Dkv​ when sequence parallelism is enabled.
  • Demb​ — divisor of the embedding / LM-head weights on one device.
  • Dbatch​ — the batch divisor: the number of device groups the replica’s batch is divided across (defined below the table).
  • GTP​, GEP​ — number of devices that take part in one TP collective and in one EP all-to-all.
  • Nreplica​ — devices in one model replica; the number of replicas a cluster of NGPUs​ devices holds is DP=⌊NGPUs​/Nreplica​⌋ (§6.1).
configurationDattn​Dexp​ (MoE)Dkv​Demb​Dbatch​GTP​GEP​Nreplica​
orthogonal + TP-attnTPTP⋅EPTP (head)TPEPTPEPPP⋅TP⋅EP⋅SP
co-located + TP-attnTPEPTP (head)TP1TPEPPP⋅max(TP,EP)⋅SP
orthogonal + DP-attn1TP⋅EPTP (seq)TPEPTPEPPP⋅TP⋅EP⋅SP
co-located + DP-attn1EPmax(TP,EP) (seq)TP1TPEPPP⋅max(TP,EP)⋅SP

Under co-location the structural constraint TP=EP holds, so max(TP,EP) and TP collapse to the same value in the co-located rows. Formulas below use these symbols directly without further repetition of the table.

Batch divisor and group batch. Under the orthogonal layout each of the EP groups carries its own copy of the attention and dense-FFN weights and its own KV cache, so the groups serve different sequences: the batch is divided Dbatch​=EP ways for everything except the expert FFN, whose tokens are routed across all TP⋅EP expert shards by the all-to-all. Without this division every group would recompute the whole batch’s attention and hold the whole batch’s KV cache, EP copies of the same work. Under co-location TP and EP are the same devices, there is one group, and Dbatch​=1. A dense model has EP=1 and therefore Dbatch​=1 in either layout. For a batch of B sequences, the group batch is the number of sequences one device group handles:

Bg​(B)=max(1,Dbatch​B​)

With fewer sequences than groups, each busy group holds one sequence and the others idle, so a device never sees a fraction of a sequence. Bg​=B whenever Dbatch​=1. The DP-attention split of the batch across the GTP​ ranks of one group is a separate division and is applied where it arises (§3.5).

Per-device Parameter Memory

Each transformer layer has two parameter groups:

  • Attention parameters Pattn​, sharded by the effective attention divisor Dattn​.
  • FFN parameters PFFN​, sharded by the effective expert/FFN divisor Dexp​. Dense FFN layers always use Dexp​=TP (no EP axis exists to overlap with), so the same formula applies to both dense and MoE FFNs given the layer-type-aware Dexp​.

For a single layer on a device, the stored parameter memory is

Mθ,layer​=Dattn​Pattn​b​+Dexp​PFFN​b​

Pipeline parallelism (PP) assigns disjoint sets of layers to different stages. Let Ls​ be the set of layers that live on PP stage s, and let Mθ,layer,ℓ​ be the per-layer memory from the expression above.

Excluding embeddings and LM head, the parameter memory per device on PP stage s is

Mθ,layers(s)​=ℓ∈Ls​∑​Mθ,layer,ℓ​

Embeddings and LM head appear only on two stages:

  • Intermediate PP stages (no embedding / LM head): Mθ,device(mid)​=Mθ,layers(mid)​

  • First PP stage (with token embedding): Mθ,device(1)​=Mθ,layers(mid)​+Demb​Pemb​b​

  • Final PP stage (with LM head): Mθ,device(PP)​=Mθ,layers(mid)​+Demb​Plm​b​

If each intermediate PP stage holds approximately L/PP layers of similar size, and we use representative per-layer values Pattn​ and PFFN​, then

Mθ,device(mid)​=PPL​Mθ,layer​=PPL​(Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+Dexp​3HINexp​​)b

For capacity planning we use a worst-case PP stage budget, adding one Demb​VH​b term to account for embedding/LM weights residing on boundary stages. Intermediate stages are slightly smaller. Therefore:

Mθ,device​=PPL​(Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+Dexp​3HINexp​​)b+Demb​VH​b

For a dense MLP model: I=Idense​, and Nexp​=EP=1 (so Dexp​=TP by definition).

For a MoE model: I=Imoe​, with Nexp​>1 and EP≥1; the lookup table above resolves Dexp​ under co-location.

Mixed MoE/Dense Architectures

Many modern architectures use a mixed design where only some layers are MoE (e.g., alternating dense and MoE layers, or MoE only in deeper layers). For such models, the parameter memory must be computed separately for dense and MoE layers, with the layer-type-aware Dexp​ resolving to TP on dense layers and to the table value on MoE layers:

Mθ,device​=Mθ,dense​+Mθ,moe​+Demb​VH​b

where:

Mθ,dense​=PPLdense​​(Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+TP3HIdense​​)b

Mθ,moe​=PPLmoe​​(Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+Dexp​3HImoe​Nexp​​)b

Dense layers use EP=1 and Nexp​=1 implicitly (FFN always TP-sharded only); MoE layers use the specified EP and Nexp​ values with Dexp​ resolved from the layout table.

Per-device Activation Memory

The per-layer working activation footprint for a batch of B sequences is B⋅(4H+2Hkv​) elements (§1.2). A device holds the working buffers of the sequences its own group serves, Bg​(B) of them.

In standard sequential layer execution, only one layer’s activation buffers are live at any time — each layer’s output overwrites the previous layer’s buffer before the next layer begins. The L/PP multiplier therefore does not appear: earlier layers’ activations are not retained while later layers execute. A 2× factor could apply when double-buffering for PP communication overlap, but this is negligible in practice and omitted.

The per-device activation memory during decoding is therefore one layer’s worth for the group batch:

Mact,device​(B)=Bg​(B)⋅(4H+2Hkv​)b

Per-device KV Cache Memory

Only attention layers produce KV cache. One sequence’s cache is sharded by the per-device head-or-sequence factor Dkv​ and additionally by SP when sequence parallelism is enabled; PP only affects how many layers are assigned to a stage. EP does not shard a sequence’s cache, but under the orthogonal layout it decides which sequences a device holds: the batch is spread over the Dbatch​ device groups, so a device holds the caches of Bg​(B) sequences and not of all B. DP does not modify the KV layout.

The semantic of Dkv​ depends on the attention mode:

  • Under TP-attn (default), Dkv​=TP and the divisor is the head-shard across the TP ranks.
  • Under DP-attn (DSv3 / SGLang), Dkv​=TP for orthogonal layout (sequence-shard across the TP ranks now acting as DP-attn ranks; per-device byte count unchanged from TP-attn) or Dkv​=max(TP,EP) for co-located layout (sequence-shard across the entire replica’s GPU set).

For a batch of B resident sequences, each carries its own KV history. We factor the per-device KV memory into a per-sequence building block MKV,token​ that captures the per-device byte cost of one sequence’s KV history (the symbol uses “token” to parallel the per-token compute and traffic terms in §2.3, §3.5 — for decode each active sequence equals one new token per step):

MKV,token​=PPL​⋅Dkv​⋅SP(2SHkv​)b​

and the per-device KV memory footprint as that block times the sequences the device’s group holds:

MKV,device​(B)=Bg​(B)⋅MKV,token​=Bg​(B)⋅PPL​⋅Dkv​⋅SP(2SHkv​)b​

which:

  • Scales linearly with B — every active sequence in the batch holds its own KV cache — at a slope of 1/Dbatch​ per device, because the batch is spread over the device groups. B here is the number of sequences resident on the replica: every stage of a pipeline holds its layers’ share of every resident sequence’s cache, so the footprint is counted at B and not at the microbatch of §7.2.
  • For long-context inference (e.g., S∈[16k,128k]), Bg​⋅S(2Hkv​)b is large enough that KV can exceed parameter memory unless aggressively reduced through Dkv​ and SP.
  • Each decoded token adds only 2Hkv​b per sequence, which is negligible compared to the pre-fill KV footprint.

Total Per-device Static Memory Footprint

Summing all the memory footprint we derive from section 1.1 - 1.4 together, we can therefore get the “minimum required” memory size for the device to host the model under a particular PP/EP/TP/SP partition.

Mdevicetotal​(B)=Mθ,device​+Mact,device​(B)+MKV,device​(B)

Note: Mθ,device​ is B-independent (weights are loaded once and shared across all sequences in the batch); Mact,device​(B) and MKV,device​(B) both scale linearly with the group batch Bg​=max(1,B/Dbatch​).

For uniform architectures (all dense or all MoE):

Mdevicetotal​=PPL​[Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+Dexp​3HINexp​​]b+Bg​⋅PPL​⋅Dkv​⋅SP2SHkv​​⋅b+Bg​(4H+2Hkv​)b+Demb​VH​b

For a dense model: I=Idense​, Nexp​=EP=1 (with Dexp​=TP).

And for a MoE model: I=Imoe​.

For mixed MoE/dense architectures (where Lmoe​<L):

Mdevicetotal​=+++​PPLdense​​[Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+TP3HIdense​​]bPPLmoe​​[Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+Dexp​3HImoe​Nexp​​]bBg​⋅PPL​⋅Dkv​⋅SP2SHkv​​⋅bBg​(4H+2Hkv​)b+Demb​VH​b​

Dense FFN keeps /TP regardless of layout (no EP axis to overlap); MoE FFN, attention weights, KV, and embeddings all use the abstract divisors with the layout table.

Note: Activation memory (Bg​(4H+2Hkv​)b, one layer at a time) and KV cache apply to all L layers. KV cache uses the total layer count L/PP since all layers’ KV tensors are concurrently resident.

2. Memory Traffic During Decoding

Section 1 quantified the static memory footprint of the model — how many bytes of parameters, KV cache, and activations must fit in device HBM.

This section instead focuses on memory traffic per decode step, i.e., the bytes that must flow between HBM and compute cores during decoding. This traffic directly determines the memory-bound component of decoding performance (Section 4’s roofline model).

Crucial Distinction for Decoding: In autoregressive decoding, each step generates one new token per active sequence (B tokens per step for a batch of B). Unlike prefill — where weights are loaded once and reused across Sinput​ tokens within a single pass — decoding reloads the entire model weight matrix from HBM every step, regardless of B. KV cache, by contrast, is read per-sequence: each of the B active sequences streams its own KV history. So per step:

  • Weight traffic (Tθ,device​): independent of B (loaded once, shared across all B tokens — equivalently, per-token weight traffic = Tθ,device​/B shrinks as B grows).
  • KV traffic: scales linearly with the number of sequences the device serves (each sequence reads its own history) — B on a single group, Bg​(B)=max(1,B/Dbatch​) when the orthogonal layout spreads the batch over Dbatch​ device groups (§1.4).

Throughout this section, the per-step traffic quantities below are consistent with this asymmetry. Optimizations like FlashAttention or Fused-MLP do not reduce weight traffic; they only reduce the traffic of intermediate activations.

This section uses the per-component effective sharding factors Dattn​, Dexp​, Dkv​, Demb​ and the batch divisor Dbatch​ of §1.4; the four-row lookup table is given there once and not repeated here. Reminder of the SP-specific adjustment: KV traffic carries an additional /SP factor on top of Dkv​ when sequence parallelism is enabled.

2.1 Model Parameter Traffic

This subsection derives the per-device weight traffic Tθ,device​. Following Section 1, we use:

  • Pattn​: Q/K/V/O projection parameters
  • PFFN​: dense FFN (or non-expert MoE core) parameters

Pemb​ is small (one row read per token) and absorbed into the embedding lookup overhead — we drop it from the steady-state traffic model. Plm​ is kept as a stage-PP-1-only term (see “LM head parameter traffic” below) — it can rival ~10% of the body for large V and warrants explicit accounting.

Attention parameter traffic

Because Pattn​ is defined per layer, a PP stage with Lstage​=L/PP layers has Lstage​Pattn​ attention parameters. These are sharded by Dattn​.

Since every weight must be read per token:

Tθ,attn​=PPL​⋅Dattn​Pattn​b​

Variant note. For Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, Pattn​ above is the per-layer MLA parameter sum from attention.md §3.3; the per-rank sharding split also differs (WDQ​, WDKV​ are not head-shared) and is given by attention.md §3.6.

FFN parameter traffic

Similarly, the FFN parameters PFFN​ are sharded by Dexp​. Although fused kernels (e.g., FlashMLP) avoid writing intermediate activations (like the gate tensor) to HBM, they still require reading the gate, up, and down projection weights fully.

Tθ,FFN​=PPL​Dexp​PFFN​​b

Final parameter-traffic expression (dense layers)

For dense layers (every weight is read every step), combining these terms:

Tθ,devicedense​=PPL​(Dattn​Pattn​​+Dexp​PFFN​​)b=PPL​(Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+TP3HIdense​​)b

(Dense FFN keeps Dexp​=TP regardless of layout, no EP axis to overlap.) For MoE layers the expert-FFN term is not the full-footprint expression; see the mixed-architecture form below.

Mixed MoE/Dense Architectures

For mixed architectures, parameter traffic is computed separately for dense and MoE layers (with dense FFN keeping Dexp​=TP regardless of layout):

Tθ,device​=Tθ,dense​+Tθ,moe​

where:

Tθ,dense​=PPLdense​​(Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+TP3HIdense​​)b

For MoE layers, per-step traffic differs from the static footprint (cf. §1.4): expert weights enter HBM traffic only for the experts the current batch actually selects, while the static footprint must hold every expert because the next step may select any of them. The conventional “all weights read each step” simplification is exact for dense layers but over-counts for MoE at small B. Writing ftouched​(B) for the expected fraction of the experts that a batch of B tokens reaches:

Tθ,moe​=PPLmoe​​(Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+Dexp​3HImoe​Nexp​​⋅ftouched​(B))b

The expert term is the rank’s expert footprint (§1.4) scaled by the touched fraction, so traffic can never exceed footprint whatever the sharding. Under the uniform-routing assumption each token selects kactive​ distinct experts out of the global pool of Nexp​, so one token misses a given expert with probability 1−kactive​/Nexp​ and all B tokens miss it with that probability to the power B:

ftouched​(B)=1−(1−Nexp​kactive​​)B

The fraction is a property of the batch and the router, not of the partition: every rank that holds a slice of a touched expert reads its slice, so by linearity of expectation the same ftouched​ applies to every rank under any tensor- or expert-parallel sharding, including layouts where a rank holds less than one whole expert (Dexp​>Nexp​).

Asymptotics:

  • Bkactive​≪Nexp​: ftouched​≈Bkactive​/Nexp​ (linear in B); traffic dominated by attention + a small expert slice.
  • Bkactive​≫Nexp​: ftouched​→1; the expression recovers the full-footprint form 3HImoe​Nexp​/Dexp​.

Under pipeline parallelism the batch in this formula is the microbatch one stage processes per pass, Bmb​ (§7.2).

Routing-uniformity caveat. Real production routers can deviate from uniform routing: load-balancing-loss anti-correlation, expert hot-spotting, or capacity-factor saturation can make some experts touched more often than others, moving ftouched​ away from the uniform-routing value at fixed B. Modeling this requires per-deployment routing statistics not generally available; the uniform-routing assumption above is documented as a known source of model inaccuracy at small B.

LM head parameter traffic

The LM head (H→V projection) is sharded by Demb​ across the vocab dimension and lives only on the last PP stage (stage PP−1). It is not divided by PP, EP, or SP. The per-step weight read on stage PP−1 is:

TLM,θ,device​=Demb​VHb​(stage PP−1 only)

Because the LM head fires once per step (not per layer), it is bookkept as a separate additive term rather than folded into the per-layer Tθ,device​. The roofline composition in §6 / §7 adds tLM​ on top of the per-stage body cost; on stages 0..PP−2 this term is zero.

2.2 Activation Traffic

This subsection covers the per-device activation traffic Tact,device​ and why the model drops it. Section 1 showed that the per-layer activation footprint for a single decoding token is small. However, without optimization, the traffic to read/write these activations—especially the S×S attention scores—would be massive (O(S2)).

The Role of FlashAttention

FlashAttention [FA1, FA2] avoids materializing the S×S score matrix in HBM by streaming the tiled attention computation through on-chip SRAM. More precisely: Q, K, V reads remain O(SH); the O(S2d2/M) score matrix IO (per [FA1] Theorem 2, where d=dhead​ and M is SRAM size) is reduced to O(S2d/M​) via tiling, compared to O(S2d) for standard attention. For large S and modern GPU SRAM sizes, this makes the O(S2) term negligible and leaves KV reads as the dominant activation traffic.

Because FlashAttention drastically reduces the score matrix traffic, the residual activation traffic (hidden-state loads/stores, FFN buffers) is O(H) per layer — negligible compared to the weight and KV cache terms for large models. We drop Tact,device​ from the traffic model here. The residual is not modelled as a term of its own: whatever it costs on a real stack is absorbed by the sustained-bandwidth factor ηβ​ when that factor is calibrated against measurement (§6.2).

2.3 KV Cache Traffic

This subsection derives the per-device KV traffic TKV,device​(B). KV cache must be fully read for each new token to compute attention against the history. For large S, the write term (appending the new token) is negligible compared to reading the history.

The per-sequence per-layer KV access is approximately:

TKV,layer​≈2SHkv​b(per sequence, per layer)

Variant note. Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) replaces 2Hkv​ above with the head-shared latent dimension (dc​+dqk,rope​), typically 25× smaller than the equivalent dense MHA. See attention.md §3.4.

KV is sharded by Dkv​ (head or sequence depending on layout/mode; see §1.4) and by SP (sequence parallelism, when enabled). Each device sees a Dkv​⋅SP1​ shard of the per-layer traffic.

We factor the per-device KV traffic into a per-token building block TKV,token​ (per-device traffic generated by one active sequence per step, summed across the L/PP layers on the stage) and an aggregator that is linear in the number of sequences the device serves. The naming parallels the per-token compute terms of §3.5 — for decode each active sequence produces one new token per step, so per-token and per-sequence coincide:

TKV,token​≈PPL​⋅Dkv​⋅SP2SHkv​b​

A device reads the histories of the sequences its own group serves. For a stage pass over a batch of B sequences — each streaming its own KV history — that is the group batch Bg​(B)=max(1,B/Dbatch​) of §1.4, and the per-step per-device KV traffic is:

TKV,device​(B)=Bg​(B)⋅TKV,token​≈Bg​(B)⋅PPL​⋅Dkv​⋅SP2SHkv​b​

The linear scaling reflects that each sequence reads its own KV cache independently. Under the co-located layout and for dense models Dbatch​=1 and this is B⋅TKV,token​; under the orthogonal layout with EP>1 a device reads only 1/EP of the batch’s histories, because the other groups hold the rest. FlashAttention does not reduce this term: keys and values from history must always be loaded to compute each sequence’s current-token attention, regardless of tiling strategy. Under pipeline parallelism the batch of a stage pass is the microbatch Bmb​ of §7.2, not the replica’s whole batch.

2.4 Total and Effective Traffic

Combining the expressions derived in Sections 2.1–2.3 (with activation traffic dropped as negligible), the effective total per-step traffic is:

Tstep,deviceeff​(B)≈Tθ,device​+TKV,device​(B)

Weight traffic is B-independent for dense layers (one load per step); KV traffic scales linearly with the group batch Bg​. Substituting yields the final fully expanded expression:

Tstep,deviceeff​(B)≈Tθ,device​ (weights, once per step)PPL​(Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+Dexp​3HINexp​​)b​​+TKV,device​(B) (KV, per sequence)Bg​⋅PPL​⋅Dkv​⋅SP2SHkv​​b​​

The first group is weight traffic (loaded once per step regardless of B), and the second is KV cache traffic (each of the Bg​ sequences the device serves reads its own history).

2.5 Static Memory Footprint vs. Memory Traffic (Important Distinction)

Sections 1 and 2 play different roles in the overall performance model:

Static Memory Footprint (Section 1) Determines whether a (DP,PP,EP,TP,SP) configuration can fit on a device (Capacity Constraint)

Mdevicetotal​≤MHBM​

Memory Traffic (Section 2) Determines the bandwidth-limited latency per decode step (Bandwidth Constraint)

tmem​(B)=BWmem​Tstep,deviceeff​(B)​

This distinction is critical: Section 1 tells us which parallelism configurations are viable, while Section 2 tells us how fast decoding can proceed for those viable configurations.

3. Compute (FLOPs) per Token

During inference, the FLOPs required to generate a token depend on the transformer layer structure. We distinguish between:

  • Prefill FLOPs (GEMM-dominant): O(S2) across the full input sequence
  • Decoding FLOPs (GEMV-dominant): O(S) for one additional token

This section focuses on decoding FLOPs, which determine TPS throughput. All FLOPs below represent per-token, per-layer, decoding FLOPs.

3.1 Q/K/V and Output Projections

Q, K, and V projections are vector–matrix multiplications of shapes:

  • Q: [1×H]⋅[H×H]
  • K: [1×H]⋅[H×Hkv​]
  • V: [1×H]⋅[H×Hkv​]
  • Output: [1×H]⋅[H×H]

Projection FLOPs

FQ​=2H2,FK​=2HHkv​,FV​=2HHkv​,FO​=2H2.

Where the factor 2 accounts for each multiply-accumulate pair in the standard GEMV convention.

Total

Fproj​=4H2+4HHkv​

If Hkv​=H (MHA), this reduces to 8H2.

Variant note. Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) replaces the projection FLOPs above with the down / up-projection cascade detailed in attention.md §3.7 (WDQ​, WUQ​, WDKV​, WO​ plus optional WUK​, WUV​ depending on execution mode). The per-step total differs structurally between materialized and absorbed modes; both are given in attention.md §3.5 (execution modes) and §3.7 (per-mode FLOP breakdown).

3.2 Attention Scores and Value Application

During decoding, the newly generated token attends to all S cached tokens in the KV cache for this layer. Conceptually, for each layer we can treat the cached keys and values as:

  • Kcache​∈RS×Hkv​
  • Vcache​∈RS×Hkv​,

where Hkv​=nkv​dhead​ is the total KV projection dimension.

Scores (Q · Kᵀ)

Each of the nq​ query heads independently computes a dot product against its corresponding (broadcast) KV head over S cached positions. Per query head: 2dhead​S FLOPs. Summed over all nq​ query heads:

Fscore​=2nq​dhead​S=2SH

GQA note: In GQA (nkv​<nq​), each KV head is shared by nq​/nkv​ query heads [GQA]. The KV cache memory scales with Hkv​ (only nkv​ unique heads are stored), but the attention FLOPs scale with H because every query head independently computes attention scores and value-weighted sums.

Value application (Attn · V)

After applying softmax to the scores, each of the nq​ query heads computes a weighted sum over the S cached values of its corresponding value head. Per head: 2dhead​S FLOPs. Total:

Fvalue​=2SH

Total KV attention FLOPs

Combining the two:

Fattn,KV​=Fscore​+Fvalue​=4SH

This term captures the sequence-length-dependent attention cost during decoding. For MHA (nkv​=nq​, Hkv​=H), this is numerically identical to the older 4SHkv​ formulation; the distinction matters for GQA/MQA models where Hkv​<H.

3.3 FFN FLOPs (Unified Dense + MoE)

To match the parameter definitions in Section 1.1, we express FFN FLOPs using a unified formulation that works for both dense FFN layers and MoE layers.

Dense FFN FLOPs

For a gated FFN (the convention assumed throughout; see §1.1), a dense FFN consists of three GEMVs:

  • a gate projection: H→I,
  • an up projection: H→I, and
  • a down (contraction) projection: I→H.

Each GEMV costs 2HD FLOPs, giving:

Fffn,dense​=6HIdense​

Convention note — gated MLPs: §1.1 counts three weight matrices for a gated FFN (gate, up, and down projections), giving PFFN​=3HI parameters. Each GEMV contributes 2HI FLOPs, so the exact total is 6HI — which this document uses throughout. The training scaling-law literature ([KAPLAN-SCALING], [CHINCHILLA]) uses 4HI, which corresponds to a non-gated 2-matrix FFN with expansion ratio 4H. Since this model targets inference of modern gated-MLP architectures (LLaMA, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral), we use the exact 6HI to ensure accurate compute-bound predictions (prefill TTFT, batched decode at B>B∗). With 6HI FLOPs and 3HI parameters, the FLOP-to-parameter ratio is exactly 2 for every weight matrix, yielding the clean OI result OI=2/b without approximation.

Dense FFN layers always have EP=1.

MoE FFN FLOPs

For MoE layers, each token is routed to k active experts (top-k gating) [DEEPSPEED-MOE]; in practice k=1 [SWITCH] or k=2 [MIXTRAL]:

  • the router is applied to the full hidden vector: Frouter​=2HNexp​ where Nexp​ is the total number of experts.

  • for each of the k selected experts for this token, the FFN computation is: Fexpert​=6HImoe​

Thus the MoE FFN FLOPs for one token in one layer are:

Fffn,moe​=Frouter​+k⋅Fexpert​=2HNexp​+k(6HImoe​)

Unified FFN FLOP Term

We now define effective FFN FLOP parameters:

  • Effective FFN “matrix” dimension: Ieff​={Idense​,kImoe​,​dense layer,MoE layer,​

  • Effective router multiplicity: Neff​={0,Nexp​,​dense layer,MoE layer.​

With these definitions, both dense and MoE FFN FLOPs can be written in a single unified form:

Fffn​=6HIeff​+2HNeff​

This matches:

  • Dense layer: Fffn​=6HIdense​+2H⋅0=6HIdense​
  • MoE layer: Fffn​=6H(kImoe​)+2HNexp​=6HImoe​k+2HNexp​

Note on MoE compute vs. traffic. The fixed factor k in Fffn,moe​ stays exact even at small B, in contrast to MoE weight traffic (§2.1 MoE weight traffic), where bytes-read-per-step depends on the expected fraction of the experts the batch reaches and is genuinely sub-linear in B. The asymmetry is the per-(token, expert) coupling: compute is independent — two tokens hitting the same expert do two separate gated MLP evaluations, so B⋅k correctly counts total expert invocations and the per-rank batched FLOPs are exactly B⋅k⋅6HImoe​/Dexp​ under uniform routing (no expectation needed). Traffic is shared — one HBM read of an expert’s weights serves all tokens hitting it that step — so it saturates sub-linearly in B and requires the touched-experts expectation formula. The same per-(token, expert) independence applies to the router term 2HNexp​, which fires once per token regardless of routing collisions.

3.4 LayerNorm and Elementwise FLOPs

LayerNorm, RMSNorm, residual additions, and elementwise ops scale linearly with H and are ~4 orders of magnitude smaller than the dominant FFN FLOPs for large models. We drop Fnorm​ from all per-device expressions. It is not modelled as a term of its own; on a measured stack it is absorbed, with every other kernel-level inefficiency, into the calibrated sustained compute rate RGPU​ (§6.2).

3.5 Per-Device FLOPs per Layer Under TP, SP, EP, and PP

For a single decoding token, the FLOPs for one transformer layer are:

Flayer​≈Fproj​+Fattn,KV​+Fffn​,

where:

  • Fproj​=4H2+4HHkv​ (Section 3.1),
  • Fattn,KV​=4SH (Section 3.2),
  • Fffn​ is dense or MoE (Section 3.3).

Fnorm​ is dropped per Section 3.4.

This subsection uses the per-component effective sharding factors and the batch divisor of §1.4; the four-row lookup table that maps layout and attention mode to factor values is given there. FLOPs-specific reminder: the KV-attention compute term Fattn,KV​ carries an additional /SP factor on top of Dkv​ when sequence parallelism is enabled.

To find per-device FLOPs, we apply sharding from each parallelism dimension and then multiply by the number of layers on the PP stage.

Tensor sharding (projections, FFN GEMMs)

The Q/K/V/O projection FLOPs follow the attention divisor:

Fprojdevice​=Dattn​Fproj​​

The FFN GEMMs follow the expert divisor:

Fffndevice​=Dexp​Fffn​​

Both are standard column- and row-parallel matmul shardings [MEGATRON]; the abstract divisors collapse to the familiar /TP (TP-attn projections), /(TP·EP) (orthogonal MoE FFN), or /EP (co-located MoE FFN) per the table above.

KV-attention sharding

The per-token attention score / value FLOPs Fattn,KV​=4SH are sharded by the same divisor that shards the KV cache itself. Under TP-attention each rank computes attention for its own heads (Dkv​=TP); under DP-attention each rank computes attention for its own sequences (Dkv​=TP orthogonal, max(TP,EP) co-located). Sequence parallelism (SP) further shards the sequence dimension within the rank [MEGATRON3]:

Fattn,KVdevice​=Dkv​⋅SP4SH​

SP does not further reduce Fproj​, Fffn​, or router FLOPs.

Expert sharding (MoE only)

EP applies only to MoE layers. Router FLOPs operate on the full hidden state and are not sharded (every token routes through the full router on every device that holds the router weights). Expert FFN GEMMs are sharded by Dexp​:

Fexpertdevice​=Dexp​k(6HImoe​)​

Dense layers always have EP=1 and Dexp​=TP.

PP (Pipeline Parallelism)

PP assigns whole layers to stages.
Each device in a PP stage owns:

PPL​ layers.

Thus:

Ftoken, device​≈PPL​(Fprojdevice​+Fattn,KVdevice​+Fffndevice​)

Total Per-device FLOPs

Dropping the negligible Fnorm​ and also substituting everything yields the final fully expanded expression per-device FLOPs for a single decoded token:

Ftoken,device​≈PPL​(Dattn​4H2+4HHkv​​+Dexp​6HIeff​​+Dkv​⋅SP4SH​+2HNeff​)

For a dense MLP model: Ieff​=Idense​,Neff​=0,EP=1 (and Dexp​=TP by definition).

For a MoE model: Ieff​=kImoe​,Neff​=Nexp​,EP≥1.

Mixed MoE/Dense Architectures

For mixed architectures, FLOPs are computed separately for dense and MoE layers (with dense FFN keeping Dexp​=TP regardless of layout):

Ftoken,device​=Fdense,device​+Fmoe,device​

Dense layer FLOPs (per device, for all dense layers on this PP stage):

Fdense,device​=PPLdense​​(Dattn​4H2+4HHkv​​+TP6HIdense​​+Dkv​⋅SP4SH​)

Note: Dense layers have no router FLOPs and use EP=1.

MoE layer FLOPs (per device, for all MoE layers on this PP stage):

Fmoe,device​=PPLmoe​​(Dattn​4H2+4HHkv​​+Dexp​6HkImoe​​+Dkv​⋅SP4SH​+2HNexp​)

Note: The router term 2HNexp​ is unsharded (applied to the full hidden state before expert selection). Prefill FLOPs (the O(S2) regime) are derived in the companion prefill document, which is not a chapter of this book.

LM head FLOPs

Mirroring the LM head traffic term in §2.1, the H→V projection is sharded by Demb​ along the vocab dimension and lives only on the last PP stage (stage PP−1). It is not divided by L, PP, or SP. A device projects the tokens of the sequences its own group serves, Bg​(B) of them (§1.4), so the per-step compute on stage PP−1 is:

FLM,step,device​(B)=Demb​2Bg​(B)HV​(stage PP−1 only)

This scales linearly with the group batch (one H→V projection per sequence) and fires once per step, not per layer. It is bookkept as a separate additive term and combined with TLM,θ,device​ into a one-shot LM-head roofline tLM​ in §6 / §7; on stages 0..PP−2 this term is zero.

Per-step (batched) FLOPs

A stage pass processes a batch of B sequences and produces 1 new token per sequence. Per-rank per-step compute scales with the number of tokens that rank actually processes, and two divisions of the batch decide that number. The first is the batch divisor of §1.4: under the orthogonal layout the batch is spread over Dbatch​=EP device groups, and a rank runs attention, the dense FFN and the router only for its own group’s Bg​(B)=max(1,B/Dbatch​) sequences. The second depends on the attention mode: DP-attention sequence-shards the group’s batch across the TP group, while TP-attention keeps the group’s batch on every rank and head-shards the attention block. To write the result, split the per-token per-device FLOPs of the expression above into four parts, each summed over the L/PP layers of the stage: the projections Fproj,token,device​ (sharded by Dattn​), the score / value term Fsv,token,device​ (sharded by Dkv​⋅SP), the home FFN work Fhome,token,device​ (dense FFN sharded by TP, plus the unsharded router), and the expert FFN Fexpert,token,device​ (MoE layers only, sharded by Dexp​). Their sum is Ftoken,device​. Each part then scales with its own batch:

  • Projections (Q/K/V/O). Under TP-attention each rank sees all Bg​ tokens of its group but does 1/Dattn​ of the per-token work (head-sharded). Under DP-attention each rank holds the full attention weight set (Dattn​=1) but processes only Bg​/GTP​ tokens (its sequence shard). The per-token formula divides by Dattn​, which is 1 under DP-attention, so the batch shard must be applied explicitly; omitting it would over-count by a factor of GTP​.
  • Score / value. The per-token term 4SH/(Dkv​⋅SP) already contains Dkv​. Under DP-attention Dkv​=GTP​ in every layout (orthogonal: Dkv​=TP; co-located: Dkv​=max(TP,EP)=TP under the structural TP=EP constraint), so the divisor already absorbs the sequence shard and the term is multiplied by the group batch Bg​ in both attention modes.
  • Home FFN (dense FFN and router gate). Computed on a token’s own group, independent of the attention mode: it scales with Bg​.
  • Expert FFN. Tokens from every device group are routed across all expert shards by the all-to-all, so each shard sees its k/Dexp​ share of every token of the batch: it scales with B, not with Bg​.

Writing the per-rank per-step compute explicitly:

Fstep,device​(B)=Bprojrank​⋅Fproj,token,device​+Bg​⋅(Fsv,token,device​+Fhome,token,device​)+B⋅Fexpert,token,device​

with the per-rank batch for the projections:

Bprojrank​={Bg​/GTP​Bg​​DP-attentionTP-attention​

When Dbatch​=1 (co-located layout, or a dense model) Bg​=B and the last two groups merge into B⋅(Fsv,token,device​+Fhome,token,device​+Fexpert,token,device​); under TP-attention the whole expression is then B⋅Ftoken,device​. Under the orthogonal layout with EP>1 only the expert FFN grows with the full batch, and the attention, dense-FFN and router work on a device is EP times smaller than a count at B would give.

This is the per-step, per-device FLOP count consumed in the roofline (§4). All downstream HW latency formulas (§4–§6) carry the (B) argument explicitly; under pipeline parallelism that argument is the microbatch Bmb​ one stage processes per pass (§7.2).

4. Compute vs. Memory Bound (Roofline Model)

Sections 2 and 3 derived the per-step memory traffic Tstep,deviceeff​(B)=Tθ,device​+Bg​⋅TKV,token​ and the per-step FLOPs per device Fstep,device​(B) of §3.5 Per-step (batched) FLOPs, both in terms of the group batch Bg​=max(1,B/Dbatch​) of §1.4. The compute roofline divides FLOPs by sustained device throughput RGPU​ (FLOPs/s):

tcompute​(B)=RGPU​Fstep,device​(B)​

In the simplest case — one device group (Dbatch​=1) under TP-attention — Fstep,device​(B)=B⋅Ftoken,device​ and Bg​=B. The operational-intensity and crossover analyses below are first written for that case and then generalized.

The memory roofline opens up across the device’s memory hierarchy. Modern accelerators expose an ordered list of memory tiers i=0,1,…,n−1 (fastest first): single-tier HBM on H100 / B200, two-tier SRAM + LPDDR5 on d-Matrix Corsair, single-tier on-die SRAM on Groq LPU. A placement policy π assigns weight and KV bytes to specific tiers, splitting Tθ,device​ into per-tier shares Tθ,0​,…,Tθ,n−1​ and TKV,device​ into TKV,0​,…,TKV,n−1​. Each tier carries its own effective bandwidth BWeff,i​=BWi​⋅ηβ,i​ (peak rate deflated by a sustained-throughput contention factor ηβ,i​∈(0,1], see sram.md §1.2) and a first-byte latency αi​ paid once per non-empty placement on that tier (the standard α–β form, treating each tier as a single transaction per step). The per-step memory time across all tiers is:

tmem​(B)=i=0∑n−1​[αi​⋅1(bytesi​>0)+BWeff,i​Tθ,i​+Bg​⋅TKV,i​​]

The αi​ floor is kept here so the device roofline matches the standard α–β form rather than a β-only shorthand. For the on-die / co-packaged tiers in scope here — SRAM, HBM, LPDDR5 — αi​ falls in the 1 ns – 200 ns range and contributes well under 0.1% of tmem​ at decode-step granularity, so dropping it for simplicity is a safe approximation in subsequent derivations. The full α–β form is also what gets reinstated in small-read regimes (paged-attention block fetch, flash-style spill — see sram.md §2.1). Tier definitions, placement policies (greedy fastest-first, operator-pinned), and worked numerical examples for d-Matrix Corsair / B200 / Groq LPU live in sram.md; this document treats Tθ,i​ and TKV,i​ as given inputs.

Single-tier reduction. When n=1 — single-tier devices like H100 / B200 / Groq LPU, or any system modeled before opening up the tier list — the sum collapses to one term:

tmem​(B)=α0​+BWeff,0​Tθ,device​+Bg​⋅TKV,token​​(n=1)

with BWeff,0​≡BWmem​. The Operational Intensity and B⋆ analyses below are written against this single-tier shorthand and additionally drop α0​ (negligible for on-die tiers) for compactness; the multi-tier crossover (weights and KV pinned to different tiers — d-Matrix Capacity Mode being the canonical example) is derived in sram.md §2.2.

tcompute​(B) is the time assuming unlimited memory bandwidth — linear in B since every sequence contributes its own per-token FLOPs. tmem​(B) is the time assuming compute is free — within each tier, weights amortize once per step (the Tθ,i​ terms are B-independent) while KV reads scale with the group batch Bg​ (each sequence the device serves reads its own history). For long-context LLMs the Bg​⋅TKV,i​ contribution summed across tiers is often dominant.

The per-step local latency on this PP stage is the roofline of the two:

tlocal​(B)=max(tcompute​(B),tmem​(B))

The asymmetric B-scaling of the two arms (compute linear in B; memory weights flat per tier, KV linear per tier) means the regime can flip with B — characterized by the operational-intensity analysis below.

Operational Intensity (Ops:Byte)

The operational intensity for decoding on this device is [ROOFLINE]:

OI(B)=Tstep,deviceeff​(B)Fstep,device​(B)​=Tθ,device​+B⋅TKV,token​B⋅Ftoken,device​​(FLOPs per byte)

The second form is the single-group, TP-attention case (Dbatch​=1); the general numerator and denominator are the Fstep,device​(B) of §3.5 and the Tstep,deviceeff​(B) of §2.4. For the single-token, single-sequence baseline (B=1), the formula collapses to OI(1)=Ftoken,device​/(Tθ,device​+TKV,token​), which establishes the fundamental memory-bound character of decode. As B grows, OI(B) rises (weight reads amortize across more sequences); the crossover-batch analysis is in the dedicated subsection below.

High-level interpretation:

  • High OI → more FLOPs per byte → compute-bound
  • Low OI → fewer FLOPs per byte → memory-bound

This rating is compared to the device’s memory-to-compute ratio (the ridge point):

BWmem​RGPU​​

If OI(B)>RGPU​/BWmem​ the step is compute-bound (and tlocal​(B)=tcompute​(B)); otherwise it is memory-bound (and tlocal​(B)=tmem​(B)).

Dominant-Term Approximation

In practice, the OI is often approximated using only the largest FLOP and traffic terms. With B sequences per step and the per-component sharding factors of §1.4:

  • Per-step FLOPs dominated by: B⋅max(Dattn​2H2​,Dexp​6HIeff​​,Dkv​⋅SP4SH​)

  • Per-step memory traffic dominated by the KV term (each sequence reads its own KV history): B⋅Dkv​⋅SP2SHkv​​b

Thus for long-context decoding (attention FLOPs dominate the FLOP max):

OI(B)≈B⋅2SHkv​/(Dkv​⋅SP)bB⋅4SH/(Dkv​⋅SP)​=Hkv​b2H​

Both B and (Dkv​⋅SP) cancel — the OI is shape- and batch-independent in this regime. (The cancellation makes intuitive sense: every sequence reads its own KV and computes its own attention, so the per-sequence FLOP-to-byte ratio is what matters; sharding splits both terms identically.)

For MHA (Hkv​=H), this reduces to 2/b. For GQA models, H/Hkv​=nq​/nkv​ amplifies the OI — e.g., for nq​/nkv​=8 (LLaMA-3 70B) the OI is 16/b. Even so, this is far below typical ridge points (~300 FLOPs/byte on H100), so long-context decode remains memory-bound in practice.

The short-context limit collapses to the same 2/b for a different reason: when weights dominate, FFN FLOPs 6HIeff​ over FFN traffic 3HIeff​⋅b also gives 2/b. So the path-independent answer is OI ≈ 2/b at B=1, with b being the only free knob.

Compute-Bound Crossover (B⋆)

The full OI(B)=B⋅Ftoken,device​/(Tθ,device​+B⋅TKV,token​) has two limiting regimes:

Memory-bound limit (B small, weight traffic dominates the denominator):

B→0lim​OI(B)=Tθ,device​B⋅Ftoken,device​​→0

At small B, the model is weight-traffic-limited. The B=1 case recovers the single-token OI established above.

Compute-bound limit (B large, KV traffic dominates the denominator):

B→∞lim​OI(B)=TKV,token​Ftoken,device​​

At large B, KV cache reads dominate and the intensity saturates at this asymptotic ceiling.

Ridge-point crossover. The crossover batch size B⋆ is the point at which the roofline transitions from memory-bound to compute-bound. Setting OI(B⋆)=RGPU​/BWmem​ (the ridge point per [ROOFLINE]) and solving:

B⋆=Ftoken,device​⋅BWmem​−TKV,token​⋅RGPU​Tθ,device​⋅RGPU​​

Existence condition. B⋆ is finite and positive iff the denominator is positive. Rearranging into ridge-point form:

B⋆<∞⟺TKV,token​Ftoken,device​​>BWmem​RGPU​​=Rridge​

i.e., the arithmetic intensity of KV traffic alone (per-token FLOPs over per-sequence KV bytes) must exceed the device ridge point. Intuition: OI(B) asymptotes to Ftoken,device​/TKV,token​ as B→∞; if this asymptotic ceiling itself sits below Rridge​, the roofline is never crossed regardless of batch size.

No-crossover regime. When the inequality is violated — typical of very long contexts on small models, where TKV,token​ grows linearly in S while Ftoken,device​ stays fixed — decode remains memory-bound at every B, and B⋆→∞. In this regime batching still amortizes weight traffic (Tθ,device​/B per token), which continues to reduce per-sequence TPOT, but it cannot push the step into the compute-bound zone; adding more sequences only adds linear KV bandwidth pressure until HBM saturates.

Weight-dominated approximation. When TKV,token​ is small relative to Tθ,device​/B⋆ (short-context decode where weight traffic dominates), B⋆ simplifies to:

B⋆≈Ftoken,device​Tθ,device​​⋅BWmem​RGPU​​(weight-dominated regime)

Intuitive interpretation: Tθ,device​/Ftoken,device​ is the inverse single-token OI (bytes per FLOP), and RGPU​/BWmem​ is the ridge point (FLOPs per byte). Their product is the batch size at which weight reuse tips the balance from memory-bound to compute-bound.

General form: pipeline depth and device groups. The derivation above is for one stage pass on a single device group. Two things change when the crossover is stated for the replica’s batch B. First, the roofline is a statement about the batch one stage processes per pass; with a full pipeline that is the microbatch Bmb​=B/PP (§7.2), so the replica-level crossover is PP times the per-pass one. Second, under the orthogonal layout a device’s compute and KV read do not grow at the full per-token rate: per in-flight sequence, attention, the dense FFN, the router and the KV read grow at the group’s share 1/Dbatch​, and only the expert FFN grows at the full rate (§3.5). With the per-sequence slopes

F′=Dbatch​Ftoken,device​−Fexpert,token,device​​+Fexpert,token,device​,TKV′​=Dbatch​TKV,token​​

the crossover batch of a replica is

B⋆=F′⋅BWmem​−TKV′​⋅RGPU​PP⋅Tθ,device​⋅RGPU​​

finite iff F′/TKV′​>Rridge​. At PP=1 and Dbatch​=1 this is the expression derived above. A stage holds 1/PP of the layers, so its weight traffic, its per-token FLOPs and its per-sequence KV read all shrink by the same factor and the per-pass crossover does not move with pipeline depth; for dense weights the replica-level crossover therefore grows in proportion to PP. For MoE layers Tθ,device​ is the weight traffic at the operating microbatch, through the touched-expert fraction of §2.1, so it is smaller in a deeper pipeline and B⋆ grows less than proportionally. On a multi-tier device BWmem​ here is the fastest tier’s effective bandwidth (the exact two-tier crossover is in sram.md §2.2). Under DP-attention the projection part of the compute slope is smaller by a further factor GTP​ (§3.5); the crossover as stated keeps the projections at their full per-token cost, which places B⋆ slightly low for projection-heavy models.

5. Communication Time During Decoding

Section 4 defined the local per-step latency on each device as the roofline of compute and the multi-tier memory sum:

tlocal​(B)=max(tcompute​(B),tmem​(B)),tmem​(B)=i=0∑n−1​BWeff,i​Tθ,i​+Bg​⋅TKV,i​​

(Single-tier devices collapse the sum to one term, recovering tmem​(B)=(Tθ,device​+Bg​⋅TKV,token​)/BWmem​ — see §4.) We now incorporate the inter-device communication time that arises during decoding under distributed parallelism. The four within-replica parallelism dimensions PP, EP, TP, SP each contribute their own per-step collective; DP has none (replicas are independent). Their physical mapping to GPUs follows the layout choice (§1.4): the orthogonal layout maps each axis to a disjoint GPU set within a replica (the canonical Megatron-LM nesting DP → PP → EP → TP → SP, outermost first), while TP+EP co-location overlays TP and EP on the same physical GPU set (DSv3 / SGLang / NVIDIA Dynamo production decode). Collective group sizes GTP​, GEP​ (§1.4) carry through identically across both layouts; the per-rank message sizes use the per-component sharding factors Dkv​, Dattn​ to absorb layout-dependent shape changes, and the group batch Bg​=max(1,B/Dbatch​) of §1.4 as the number of sequences whose activations a collective carries.

All communication costs follow the standard α–β latency model [ALPHA-BETA]:

tcomm​=α+Beff​message size​

where α is the collective or hop latency, and Beff​ is the sustained bandwidth of the communication path.

The parameters α and Beff​ in this model are not abstract: they are topology-dependent physical properties of the underlying interconnect. Different parallelism domains—TP, EP, SP, and PP—may be mapped to different network fabrics or different portions of the same physical topology (e.g., NVSwitch star within a node, 2D/3D torus across nodes, or hybrid switch-plus-fabric designs). Consequently, each collective type sees its own communication characteristics, with potentially different latency constants and effective bandwidths. To keep the analysis general, we denote these as αXP​ and Beff,XP​ for TP, EP, SP, and PP respectively. Their actual numerical values depend on the system’s physical layout, routing scheme, and bisection bandwidth properties (e.g., constant-hop NVSwitch vs. hop-scaling torus fabrics). The following sections therefore use αXP​ and Beff,XP​ as collective-specific, topology-aware parameters, to be instantiated according to the actual deployment mapping.

Delegation to the collective-communication tutorial. Citations of the form collectives/NN_name.md in this chapter refer to the chapters of the separate collective-communication tutorial, which is not part of this book; the Collective Communication page links to it. The shipped collective primitives (ring AR, double binary tree AR, ring AG / RS, pairwise A2A on star; dim-decomposed ring and bisection-bound A2A on torus; hierarchical RS → sub-AR → AG; in-network reduction via NVLS / Quantum SHARP / Tomahawk Ultra) are cost-modeled in collectives/01_collective_algorithms.md (per-algorithm) and collectives/02_topology_mapping.md (star / torus / mesh), with hierarchical composition in collectives/03_hierarchical_topologies.md, in-network primitives in collectives/04_in_network_collectives.md, and contention coefficients (ηα​,ηβ​) in collectives/05_contention_and_congestion.md; the cheatsheet at collectives/00_summary.md indexes all of these. This section instantiates those primitives with the decode-scale per-rank message sizes defined below; derivations and the (αsum​,BWmin​) tier-chain accumulation live there. The αXP​ and BWXP​ values used below are span quantities: a collective whose group of G ranks reaches across several switching tiers of its fabric pays the sum of the crossed tiers’ startup latencies, and its bandwidth is that of the narrowest crossed tier. On a single-tier fabric they are simply that tier’s latency and per-port bandwidth, independent of G.

Message sizes and their shard structure

To remain consistent with the compute and memory models, we strictly define the payload size for each collective type. Note the distinction between storage size (sharded) and communication payload (often full-width). Each shape below is given per step for the group batch Bg​, the sequences one device group handles in one stage pass (§1.4): under the orthogonal layout each of the EP groups runs its collectives over its own B/EP sequences, and under co-location or for a dense model Bg​=B. The per-token shape is the per-step shape divided by Bg​. Under pipeline parallelism the batch of a stage pass is the microbatch of §7.2.

  • PP (Pipeline Parallel): Per-rank payload Bg​⋅H/Dkv​ per step. Rationale: High-performance PP (e.g., Megatron-LM) preserves cross-section rank alignment, so each device only forwards its local share of the activation to the corresponding rank in the next stage. Under TP-attention this is the head-shard (H/TP per token); under DP-attention it is the sequence shard (1/Dkv​ of the Bg​ sequences, each carrying full H). Both reduce to a per-rank PP payload of Bg​⋅H/Dkv​ per step.

  • EP (Expert Parallel): Per-rank logical payload Bg​⋅k⋅H per step (with the standard (GEP​−1)/GEP​ factor in the all-to-all cost form distributing this across peers). Rationale: MoE routing sends token activations to experts. While the traffic is bidirectional (Dispatch + Combine), we model this by applying a factor of 2 to the collective steps in Section 5.2 rather than doubling the base message size here.

  • TP (Tensor Parallel): Per-rank logical payload Bg​⋅H per step (under both AR and AG primitives — AG carries the same total bytes, the per-rank shard Bg​⋅H/GTP​ is what each rank initially holds before the AG fans it out). Rationale: Row-Parallel matrix multiplication produces a vector of partial sums of full width H (TP-attn AR), or each rank already holds the full attention output for its sequence subset and the AG redistributes it to the TP-sharded form for the next FFN block (DP-attn AG).

  • SP (Sequence Parallel): Per-rank payload Bg​⋅H/Dkv​ per step, independent of the context length S. Rationale: Decode sends each sequence’s new query to the ranks that hold the KV shards and merges the partial attention outputs back (the pass-Q variant of ring attention, §5.4), so the payload is the query-side activations and not the cache. The alternative that circulates the KV blocks themselves (pass-KV) carries Bg​⋅S⋅2Hkv​/Dkv​ cache elements per rank per layer and is the prefill choice.

5.1 Pipeline Parallel (PP) Hop

Pipeline Parallelism (PP) forwards activations from one pipeline stage to the next [MEGATRON3]. Because TP is nested inside PP, high-performance implementations (e.g., Megatron-LM PP, DeepSpeed PP, NVIDIA NeMo, and FasterTransformer) preserve the TP rank alignment across all PP stages. That is, TP rank i in stage s corresponds directly to TP rank i in stage s+1.

This alignment has an important consequence:
each device only needs to forward its local share of the hidden state to the rank-aligned device on the next stage, not a full H-dimensional vector. The full activation is conceptually transferred across the PP boundary, but it is split naturally across Dkv​ separate device-to-device links (where Dkv​ is the head- or sequence-shard divisor of §1.4; under TP-attention this is the head shard, under DP-attention the sequence shard).

Thus the PP hop behaves as a single, shard-sized point-to-point transfer with per-rank message size ≈H/Dkv​ per token. For a stage pass in which the device’s group handles Bg​ sequences (§1.4), the per-step payload scales linearly:

tPP​(B)=αPP​+BWPP​Bg​⋅(H/Dkv​)b​

The α-term (single point-to-point latency) is paid once per hop regardless of payload; only the β-term scales with the batch. This shard-preserving PP design avoids the extra TP collectives that would be required if stages exchanged full activations and then re-sharded them. Maintaining cross-section rank consistency across stages therefore yields a significantly faster pipeline, and is the standard strategy in modern LLM training and inference systems.

Tier-aware PP cost (nested-layout convention). αPP​ and BWPP​ above are not uniformly tier-0 fabric values. They are the latency and bandwidth of the specific tier the PP boundary physically crosses, which depends on where PP sits in the nested layout DP → PP → EP → TP → SP (innermost = highest-bandwidth tier). The per-axis tier assignment walks the fabric chain inner→outer, allocating each axis to the smallest tier whose cumulative reach holds the cumulative product of inner axes × this axis. For example, on d-Matrix squadrack (3-tier chain: 16 × 4 × 8):

  • PP=2,TP=8: cumulative 8⋅2=16≤ tier-0 cap → PP at tier 0 (pair-of-cards mesh, α=0.115 μs, BW=64 GB/s).
  • PP=8,TP=8: cumulative 8⋅8=64≤ tier-1 cap → PP at tier 1 (PCIe, α=0.65 μs).
  • PP=32,TP=8: cumulative 8⋅32=256>64 → PP at tier 2 (Ethernet, α=2.0 μs, BW=50 GB/s).

On single-tier systems (e.g., NVL72), every axis collapses to tier 0 and the legacy tier-0 PP pricing is recovered exactly. This is a worst-case-tier model — within a single PP cost call the outermost tier the boundary could possibly cross is used. A finer per-hop blend (some boundaries within tier 0, some across tier 1) is left as a future refinement; the worst-case form matches the conservative engineering view that “PP runs across servers” for sweeps where it does.

5.2 Expert Parallel (EP) All-to-All (MoE Dispatch and Combine)

MoE layers require exchanging token activations across the expert-parallel (EP) dimension via all-to-all routing [DEEPSPEED-MOE]. EP communication follows a bidirectional dispatch-and-combine pattern: token activations are routed from the source rank to the rank holding the selected expert (top-k), and the expert’s output is then sent back to the source rank to be added to the residual stream. We model these as two distinct A2A collectives per MoE layer (nEP​=2 in §5.5), each costing one single-direction A2A — this aligns the cost-model bookkeeping with the kernel-launch counter (§7.1), since dispatch and combine are also two separate NCCL API calls.

Let k denote the number of active experts per token. Each direction carries a kHb byte per-rank per-token payload; for a stage pass in which the rank’s group handles Bg​ sequences the per-step payload is Bg​⋅kHb. The collective group size is GEP​ of §1.4 (equal to EP across all four configurations). The shipped A2A primitive is pairwise direct-send (NCCL on star; bisection-bound pairwise on torus). Bruck / log-hop A2A does not ship and does not appear in the cost — see collectives/01_collective_algorithms.md §7 for the primitive derivations. On a star topology, the per-direction A2A cost is:

tEP​(B)=(GEP​−1)αEP​+GEP​GEP​−1​⋅BWEP​Bg​⋅kHb​

§5.5’s per-layer accumulator multiplies this by nEP​=2 to recover the full Dispatch + Combine cost. For torus EP fabrics, substitute the bisection-bound form of collectives/02_topology_mapping.md §3 with M=Bg​⋅kHb. For dense models (EP=GEP​=1), tEP​(B)=0.

Note on expectation under uniform routing. Unlike MoE weight traffic (§2.1), where bytes-read-per-step is the footprint scaled by the expected fraction of touched experts and is genuinely sub-linear in B at small B, the per-rank A2A send / receive volume above is the deterministic GEP​GEP​−1​⋅Bg​kHb. Each token-expert assignment generates its own dispatch payload regardless of routing collisions — two tokens hitting the same expert send two separate hidden vectors — so the β-side scales exactly linearly in B with no expectation correction. The same independence applies to TP, SP, and PP collectives in §5.3–§5.5: their payloads are deterministic by construction (every rank participates in every collective every step), and the expectation question does not arise. The only place expectation would tighten the EP A2A model is the number of active destination links at extremely small Bg​⋅k<GEP​ — when some destination ranks receive zero tokens that step. We omit this correction: the regime is rare in production decode (running EP this wide at B this small has no throughput justification), the α-cost dominates the budget at small B anyway, and the resulting overestimate is bounded by (GEP​−E[active dests])⋅αEP​ — typically well under 1% of tstep​.

Co-located note. Under the co-located layout the GEP​ ranks share physical GPUs with the GTP​ ranks. The all-to-all wire payload per call is unchanged (still Bg​⋅kHb per direction across GEP​ ranks), but the EP A2A and any TP collective on the same physical GPUs cannot run concurrently — they share the NVLink bandwidth and serialize at the fabric layer. This shows up in the §5.5 per-stage accumulator naturally because TP and EP collectives are already accumulated sequentially.

Two A2A data-flow patterns under DP-attention

Under DP-attention, the activations entering the MoE block come from GTP​ separately-batched attention replicas (each rank holds Bg​/GTP​ tokens of attention output, since the batch is split across the GTP​ DP-attention ranks while attention parameters are replicated on each rank). Two production patterns exist for how these per-rank tokens are routed through the MoE all-to-all (A2A); they differ by a factor of GTP​ in the per-rank dispatch payload, which dominates EP cost at large B:

  • Gather-then-dispatch. Insert a TP all-gather before the MoE block to bring the group’s full Bg​ tokens onto every rank, then dispatch from the full Bg​. Per-rank dispatch payload Mdisp​=Bg​⋅kHb. Per-rank combine payload symmetrically Bg​⋅kHb. Adds one TP all-gather per MoE layer at Bg​⋅Hb payload (the post-attention AG already counted in §5.3 — under this pattern the AG serves both the FFN and the MoE input). This is the conservative pattern shipped by general-purpose MoE backends that assume the residual stream is replicated across TP ranks before any sparse-block compute. Total per-rank wire bytes per MoE layer ≈ Bg​⋅Hb⋅(1+2k).

  • Scatter-direct. Skip the AG; the dispatch A2A operates directly on the per-rank Bg​/GTP​ attention-sharded tokens, routing each token to its k destination experts wherever they live across the GEP​ ranks. Per-rank dispatch payload Mdisp​=(Bg​/GTP​)⋅kHb — a factor of GTP​ smaller. The combine returns the expert outputs back to the originating attention rank, payload symmetrically (Bg​/GTP​)⋅kHb. No AG fires before MoE; the residual stays sharded across attention ranks throughout the layer. This is the pattern shipped by DeepEP [DEEPEP] and the SGLang DeepEP integration [SGLANG-DPATTN], which expose dispatch APIs parameterized by per-rank token counts rather than a globally-gathered batch. Total per-rank wire bytes per MoE layer ≈ 2(Bg​/GTP​)⋅kHb — i.e. a GTP​⋅(1+2k)/(2k) reduction over gather-then-dispatch (~GTP​× for typical k).

The cost-model formulas in this section are written for the gather-then-dispatch pattern (the conservative ceiling) so that Mdisp​=Bg​⋅kHb. To model scatter-direct, substitute Bg​→Bg​/GTP​ in the EP A2A formulas of this section and drop both TP collectives of every MoE layer from §5.5: the all-gather before the MoE block and the all-reduce after it, since the dispatch works on the per-rank shards and the combine returns the expert outputs to the same shards.

Trade-offs. Scatter-direct is unambiguously smaller in bytes-on-wire and is the production-favored pattern for very-large-B DSv3-class deployments where MoE comm would otherwise dominate. The cost is in ergonomics and fabric assumptions: it requires the MoE backend to be written with sharded-token awareness (variable per-rank token counts after routing, no implicit “I have the full residual” assumption), pairs naturally with hook-based dispatch / combine kernels that overlap the A2A with expert compute on a separate stream rather than blocking, and the high-throughput kernels assume bisection-bandwidth-class fabrics (intra-NVLink-island today; cross-node paths use Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) transports with their own latency floor). Gather-then-dispatch remains the right model when these assumptions don’t hold — small GTP​ where the AG is cheap, MoE backends without sharded-token support, or fabrics where the AG ride-along to the FFN amortizes the cost.

5.3 Tensor Parallel (TP) Communication

TP groups compute each layer in parallel across GTP​ devices (group size from §1.4; GTP​=TP across all four configurations) using column- and row-parallel linear layers [MEGATRON]. Each layer fires two TP collectives: one in the attention block (after the output projection) and one in the MLP / MoE expert block (after the down projection). The collective in the attention block depends on the attention parallelism mode:

  • TP-attention (default): all-reduce (AR) — sums partial outputs across the GTP​ ranks that each hold a shard of the heads.
  • DP-attention: all-gather (AG) — each rank already holds the full attention output for its assigned sequence subset; the AG gathers all sequences’ hidden states so the downstream TP-sharded FFN can run [DSV3, SGLANG-DPATTN].

The MLP / MoE block always fires an AR (it is TP-sharded under both attention modes).

Critical Note on Message Size: unlike PP (which sends a shard), the TP collectives operate on the full hidden state vector (H). Each device owns only a shard of the weights, but the post-row-parallel output (or pre-FFN gathered hidden state) is a vector of size H that must be moved globally; the payload is Hb bytes per token, not (H/GTP​)b. For a stage pass in which the group handles Bg​ sequences the per-step payload is Bg​⋅Hb.

NCCL ships two algorithms on a star fabric for both AR and AG — ring (large-M) and double binary tree (DBT, small-M). The schedule is fixed by the software stack or chosen as the cheapest candidate for the partition and batch (see “Practical Guidance: Shipped Algorithm Selection” at the end of this section and collectives/02_topology_mapping.md §2). Both are pipelined and bandwidth-optimal; only the nα​ coefficient differs. For the decode payload M=Bg​⋅Hb, the per-call costs are:

tTP,ARring​(B)=2(GTP​−1)αTP​+2⋅GTP​GTP​−1​⋅BWTP​Bg​⋅Hb​

tTP,AGring​(B)=(GTP​−1)αTP​+GTP​GTP​−1​⋅BWTP​Bg​⋅Hb​

The AG cost is exactly half the AR cost (one pass through the ring instead of the AR’s two: reduce-scatter then all-gather). The DBT variants substitute 2⌈log2​GTP​⌉⋅αTP​ (AR) or ⌈log2​GTP​⌉⋅αTP​ (AG) for the α-side coefficient; the β-side terms are unchanged. For torus TP fabrics (dim-decomposed ring, shipped on TPU / Trainium), substitute the torus AR / AG forms of collectives/02_topology_mapping.md §3 with M=Bg​⋅Hb. Derivation and the ring-vs-DBT empirical crossover behavior are in collectives/02_topology_mapping.md §2.

The per-layer TP cost depends on attention mode and is assembled into the per-stage budget in §5.5.

5.4 Sequence Parallel (SP) Communication

Sequence Parallelism (SP) in inference typically refers to Ring Attention [RING-ATTN]: the KV cache is partitioned along the sequence dimension S across SP ranks. Two exact variants exist, and which one is cheap depends on how many query tokens there are [YANG-CP-2024]:

  • Pass-KV. The queries stay local and the KV blocks travel round the ring, so every rank ends up attending over the full history. The traffic is the whole KV cache. This is the right choice when the queries are as numerous as the keys — a full prefill.
  • Pass-Q. The queries travel to the ranks that hold the KV shards; each rank attends over its own shard and the partial attention outputs are merged back at the query’s home rank. The traffic is the queries and their partial outputs. This is the right choice when the queries are few and the cache is large — decode, where each sequence contributes one new token, and partial prefill with a high cache-hit rate.

[YANG-CP-2024] uses pass-Q for decode and pass-KV for full prefill, and the model follows it: decode is costed as pass-Q, prefill as pass-KV. (Pass-KV remains available for decode as an option; it reproduces the cost of gathering the whole cache on every layer of every token, which is why it is not the default.) DeepSpeed-Ulysses [DEEPSPEED-ULYSSES] is an alternative SP approach using all-to-all instead of ring; unlike ring, it is bounded by the number of attention heads rather than the number of devices.

SP Communication Latency (decode, pass-Q)

Each sequence’s new query visits the SP ranks and its partial outputs come back and are combined — a broadcast followed by a reduce, which has the volume and step count of one all-reduce over the SP group. The per-rank payload is the query-side activations of the group’s batch, MSP​(B)=Bg​⋅(H/Dkv​)⋅bact​, independent of the context length S. Substituting into the ring all-reduce cost of collectives/01_collective_algorithms.md:

tSP​(B)=2(SP−1)αSP​+2SPSP−1​⋅BWSP​Bg​⋅(H/Dkv​)⋅bact​​

For comparison, the pass-KV variant gathers MSP​(B)=Bg​⋅S⋅(2Hkv​/Dkv​)⋅bkv​ per rank per layer (the gathered-output convention of the all-gather primitive) — larger than the pass-Q payload by a factor of order S⋅Hkv​/H, which is thousands at production context lengths.

Decode overlap note: in single-token decode, per-token compute time is small, so communication overlap with compute (ρcomm​) is unlikely to be significant for SP. The unified ρcomm​ in §6.2 applies to all collective traffic; if SP dominates the comm budget on a given config, calibrate ρcomm​ down accordingly rather than zeroing it per-axis (the cost model has no per-axis ρcomm​ knob).

5.5 Total Communication Time Per Step on a PP Stage

Sections 5.1–5.4 provide per-step, per-layer communication costs for each parallelism axis (TP, EP, SP), and a per-step, per-hop cost for PP. Each carries the (B) argument explicitly: α-side stays constant in B (one collective per layer per stage regardless of payload), β-side scales linearly with the group batch Bg​(B). We now combine them into the total per-step communication time on a given pipeline-parallel (PP) stage.

Per-layer vs. per-stage normalization

A Transformer layer contains exactly one Attention block and one MLP/MoE block. Each block triggers a fixed number of communication collectives, and within each layer, TP, EP, and SP collectives are strictly ordered:

  • Attention block

    • 1 TP collective at the attention → FFN transition. The primitive depends on attention mode: all-reduce (AR) under TP-attention (default), all-gather (AG) under DP-attention. Per-call cost is tTP,AR​(B) or tTP,AG​(B) from §5.3.
    • 1 SP collective (if SP is enabled).

  • MLP / MoE block

    • 1 TP all-reduce at the FFN / expert output projection (always AR; not affected by attention mode).
    • 2 EP all-to-all calls (Dispatch + Combine; MoE layers only).

This gives the per-layer NCCL API call counts: nTP​=2 (one in attention, one in FFN/expert), nEP​=2 (Dispatch + Combine on MoE layers, 0 on dense layers), nSP​=1 (when SP is enabled, 0 otherwise). These counts are layout- and mode-independent — they describe how many distinct collective calls fire per layer, not how expensive each call is. The per-call cost is what splits by mode (AR vs AG inside tTPattn​). Kernel-launch accounting in §7.1 reuses these n∗​ counts.

These collectives must complete before the token can advance to the next layer. Since a PP stage contains L/PP sequential layers and TP, EP, and SP operations within each layer depend on one another (e.g., TP → SP in attention and EP → TP in MoE), they are strictly sequential and do not overlap. The per-layer TP cost is the sum of one attention TP collective and one FFN TP all-reduce:

tTPlayer​(B)=tTPattn​(B)+tTP,AR​(B),tTPattn​(B)={tTP,AR​(B)tTP,AG​(B)​TP-attentionDP-attention​
