Switching from TP-attn to DP-attn replaces the attention AR with an AG, saving tTP,AR​(B)−tTP,AG​(B)=(GTP​−1)αTP​+(GTP​−1)/GTP​⋅Bg​⋅Hb/BWTP​ per layer (one AG’s worth of α + bandwidth, since AG is half the cost of AR).

Adding PP hop cost

The PP hop is different: it is a per-step, per-hop cost rather than a per-layer cost. A step’s microbatch is forwarded once from PP stage s to stage s+1, with latency tPP​(B) as defined in Section 5.1.

The total per-step communication time on this stage is:

tcomm​(B)=PPL​(tTPlayer​(B)+nSP​tSP​(B))+PPLmoe​​(nEP​tEP​(B))+tPP​(B)

where nEP​=2 (dispatch + combine), nSP​=1 (when SP is enabled, 0 otherwise), and tTPlayer​(B) is mode-dependent as above.

Interpretation

  • The first term accumulates TP and SP collectives required by all L/PP layers on this PP stage (both dense and MoE layers have attention blocks requiring these collectives). The TP collective’s primitive split (AR + AR under TP-attn, AG + AR under DP-attn) is encoded inside tTPlayer​(B).
  • The second term accumulates EP collectives required only by the Lmoe​/PP MoE layers on this PP stage. Dense layers do not require EP communication.
  • The third term accounts for the one PP hop that forwards the step’s microbatch to the next stage.
  • This combined expression represents the total communication work per step for the stage. Whether this communication becomes the latency bottleneck or is hidden by overlap is addressed in Section 4’s roofline-style model and Section 6’s end-to-end pipeline analysis.

Mixed MoE/Dense Architectures

For architectures where only some layers are MoE (e.g., Lmoe​<L), the EP communication cost is proportionally reduced. This is particularly important for models like DeepSeek-V2 or Mixtral variants that alternate between dense and MoE layers.

For a pure dense model: Lmoe​=0, so the EP term vanishes entirely.

For a pure MoE model: Lmoe​=L, recovering the original formula.

Summary of Collective Types and Message Sizes

ParallelismOccurs inCollective TypeCalls/layerMessage Size (per device, per step)Layer Types
PPbetween layerspoint-to-point1Bg​⋅(H/Dkv​)bAll
TP (attn)attention outputAR (TP-attn) or AG (DP-attn)1Bg​⋅HbAll
TP (FFN)MLP / expert outputAR1Bg​⋅HbAll
EPMoE FFNall-to-all2Bg​⋅kHbMoE only
SPattentionpass-Q round trip, costed as a ring all-reduce1Bg​⋅(H/Dkv​)bAll

At Bg​=1 these reduce to the classical single-token payloads. The Bg​ factor reflects that a device group processes Bg​ activations concurrently in one stage pass, so each collective carries Bg​× the per-token activation vector: Bg​=max(1,B/Dbatch​) for a pass over B sequences (§1.4), with B the microbatch Bmb​ under pipeline parallelism (§7.2).

Practical Guidance: Shipped Algorithm Selection

Each collective in this section uses the algorithm that is actually shipped on the target fabric; other algorithms (Bruck A2A, recursive-doubling AR, PAT AG) are reference-only and live in collectives/01_collective_algorithms.md Appendix B. Selection rules:

  • TP All-Reduce: NCCL ships both ring and double binary tree (DBT) on a star fabric (collectives/02_topology_mapping.md §2). The schedule is either fixed by the software stack or chosen per partition and batch as the one with the lowest modeled cost, which is how NCCL itself selects: it predicts a time for every enabled algorithm and takes the minimum [NCCL-TUNING]. On torus fabrics (TPU / Trainium), only dim-decomposed ring ships and there is no choice to make. Empirical crossover: DBT wins at small M, ring wins at large M ([DEMYST-NCCL]).

  • In-network collectives (INC): where a switch tier can reduce or replicate in the fabric, the in-network form is one more candidate, not an obligation. It is used when it is cheaper than the software schedule and skipped when it is not, again matching NCCL, where the NVLink SHARP path is one entry in the same minimum-time selection [NCCL-TUNING]. Inside one switch domain it nearly always wins. On a group that spans two fabric tiers it is applied per phase of the hierarchical schedule, as collectives/03_hierarchical_topologies.md §3.1 composes it: the reduce-scatter (RS) and all-gather (AG) inside each inner island run on the inner switch, and the sub-all-reduce across islands, which carries only the reduced 1/Ginner​ payload, runs on the outer one. A tier without the capability keeps its software phase. The alternative of one flat transaction through the whole aggregation tree moves the full payload over the narrowest link; it is kept as a candidate because it wins at very small payloads, where one switch round trip beats three, and it loses by a wide margin once the payload is large and the outer tier is much slower than the inner one.

  • Idealized flat reference fabrics: a multi-tier fabric is given the hierarchical schedule, whose hop count is roughly the island size plus the island count, while a single-tier fabric is given one ring or tree over the whole group. A hypothetical flat fabric built as an upper bound for a tiered one can therefore price above it, most visibly for the ring all-gather, which has no log-depth form. A switch that reaches every rank in one hop can run any grouping, so such a reference fabric is allowed to group its ranks into islands of the tiered fabric’s inner radix and take the cheaper of the flat and the grouped schedule. Real single-tier systems do not use this option: on them a ring means one ring.

  • EP All-to-All: NCCL ships pairwise direct-send on a star; TPU / Trainium ships the bisection-bound pairwise form on a torus (collectives/01_collective_algorithms.md §7). Log-hop (Bruck) A2A is not shipped and does not appear in this section’s formulas.

  • SP collective: decode’s pass-Q round trip (§5.4) is costed as a ring all-reduce over the SP group. The pass-KV variant, used for prefill and available for decode as an option, is a ring all-gather: KV shards are large and must be processed in sequence order, so tree variants are impractical. This applies to both star (collectives/01_collective_algorithms.md §6) and torus (collectives/02_topology_mapping.md §3).

See collectives/00_summary.md §4–§7 for the full shipped-primitive inventory and per-topology cost formulas (including hierarchical RS → sub-AR → AG and in-network reduction); collectives/05_contention_and_congestion.md for the contention coefficients (ηα​,ηβ​).

6. Partition Strategy and Hardware Latency

This chapter brings memory, compute, and communication together at the per-stage level. It produces tstage,hw​, the hardware-intrinsic GPU-side step time, and the HBM-feasibility constraint that gates which partitions are even runnable. Two axes are covered:

  1. Feasible model partitioning via HBM limits (§6.1)
  2. Local per-token latency via the compute–memory roofline plus collective overlap (§6.2)

§7 layers scheduling and software costs on top of tstage,hw​(B) to produce the user-observed metrics: it derives the pipeline traversal and kernel-launch overhead that turn tstage,hw​(B) into tstep,user​(B) (and the throughput metrics TPS / TTPS). Time to first token (TTFT) is derived in the companion prefill document, which is not a chapter of this book; its composition is summarized in framework.md §3 and disaggregation.md.

6.1 Model Partition Strategy from HBM Constraints

A parallel configuration (DP,PP,EP,TP,SP) together with the layout / attention-mode choice (§1.4) is feasible only if each device can store:

  • its parameter shard,
  • its KV-cache shard, and
  • the activation workspace needed for a single decoding token,

within the available HBM capacity MHBM​.

This subsection uses the per-component effective sharding factors Dattn​, Dexp​, Dkv​, Demb​ and the group batch Bg​=max(1,B/Dbatch​) from §1.4 above. Replica counting uses one additional per-layout quantity, Nreplica​ (the number of devices one model replica occupies), repeated here from the §1.4 table for the partition-strategy derivations below:

layout and attention modeNreplica​
orthogonal + TP-attnPP⋅TP⋅EP⋅SP
co-located + TP-attnPP⋅max(TP,EP)⋅SP
orthogonal + DP-attnPP⋅TP⋅EP⋅SP
co-located + DP-attnPP⋅max(TP,EP)⋅SP

The two co-located rows collapse to the same Nreplica​ formula because TP=EP structurally under co-location.

We define the total per-device static footprint as

Mdevicetotal​(B)=Mθ,device​+Mact,device​(B)+MKV,device​(B)≤MHBM​

Using the per-device memory expressions derived in Section 1, the fully expanded form for uniform architectures is:

PPL​[Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+Dexp​3HINexp​​+Bg​⋅Dkv​⋅SP2SHkv​​]b+Bg​(4H+2Hkv​)b+Demb​VH​b≤MHBM​

where:

  • the bracketed term is the intermediate PP-stage footprint of the parameters and of the KV cache; the KV term carries the group batch Bg​ because every sequence the device’s group holds brings its own cache (§1.4), and the term after the bracket is the activation workspace of those Bg​ sequences.
  • B is the number of sequences resident on the replica; under the orthogonal layout a device holds Bg​=B/EP of them, so the same device memory admits EP times the batch that a count at B would allow.
  • and the final Demb​VH​b term models the worst-case embedding / LM-head overhead on boundary PP stages.
  • for a dense MLP model: I=Idense​, and Nexp​=EP=1 (so Dexp​=TP).
  • for a MoE model: I=Imoe​, with Nexp​>1 and EP≥1.

For mixed MoE/dense architectures, the memory constraint uses the split formula from Section 1.4, where dense and MoE layer contributions are computed separately.

Calculating DP for a Fixed Total HBM Capacity

The total Data Parallelism degree (DP) is constrained by both the total cluster size (NGPUs​) and the memory headroom available on each device.

  1. Memory Headroom Requirement: DP scaling is only possible if Mdevicetotal​≤MHBM​ for the chosen inner sharding degrees (PP,EP,TP,SP) and layout / attention-mode choice.
  2. Replication Logic: Each model replica requires a dedicated group of Nreplica​ devices (§1.4; layout-dependent).

Let NGPUs​ be the total number of devices in the cluster. The maximum achievable DP count is:

DP=⌊Nreplica​NGPUs​​⌋

with Nreplica​=PP⋅TP⋅EP⋅SP under the orthogonal layout and Nreplica​=PP⋅max(TP,EP)⋅SP under co-location. This flat count holds when the whole cluster is one switching domain. On a tiered fabric the count respects islands (a box or a rack): the unit whose collectives are priced on the inner tier is one pipeline stage’s block of Nreplica​/PP devices, so a block must sit whole inside an island while consecutive stages may sit in different islands. A system of Nislands​ islands of Nisland​ devices holds Nislands​⋅⌊Nisland​/(Nreplica​/PP)⌋ blocks, DP is that number divided by PP and rounded down, and the devices left over in each island idle. Eight 72-device racks hold eight 64-device blocks — eight single-stage replicas or four two-stage ones — not the nine and four that the flat formula gives.

Physical Interpretation:

  • Scaling Limit: To increase DP for higher throughput (TTPS), one must either add more total GPUs to the cluster or increase inner sharding (e.g., higher PP or SP) to reduce Mdevicetotal​, though the latter consumes more devices per replica.
  • Footprint vs. Replica Count: There is a direct trade-off: higher sharding degrees “thin out” the memory footprint per device to fit large context S or large models, but they simultaneously reduce the number of independent replicas that can fit in a fixed cluster.
  • Co-location’s replica-shrink effect: Switching to TP+EP co-location drops Nreplica​ from PP⋅TP⋅EP⋅SP to PP⋅max(TP,EP)⋅SP — at TP=EP=8 this is an 8× reduction (from 64 GPUs to 8 GPUs per replica), correspondingly multiplying DP for the same cluster size. The cost is that each device must now hold 1/EP of the experts (rather than 1/(TP⋅EP)), and that the batch is no longer divided across EP device groups (Dbatch​=1), so each device serves the replica’s whole batch; see §6.3 for when this trade pays.

6.2 Local and Networking Per-Step Latency

All quantities below are per stage pass, with B sequences batched together in the pass. They are restatements of the building blocks from §3–§5 with B threaded explicitly; a device group handles Bg​=max(1,B/Dbatch​) of those sequences (§1.4), and under pipeline parallelism B is the microbatch Bmb​ of §7.2.

Compute-bound latency

tcompute​(B)=RGPU​Fstep,device​(B)​

with Fstep,device​(B) from §3.5 (B⋅Ftoken,device​ for a single device group under TP-attention).

RGPU​ is the precision-aware compute peak. The reference figure for a device is its dense 16-bit peak, and the peak at a working precision of b bytes per parameter follows the byte ratio, RGPU​(b)=RGPU​(2)⋅2/b: halving the operand width doubles the operations per second. This holds for the GPU and TPU families modeled here. A device whose published peaks do not follow the byte ratio carries them as a per-precision table that replaces the rule. d-Matrix Corsair is the case in scope: its vendor figures are 600, 2400 and 9600 TFLOPs per card at 16, 8 and 4 bits, a factor of four per halving [DMATRIX-BRIEF], so the byte-ratio rule anchored at 8 bits would under-state its 4-bit peak by 2× and over-state its 16-bit peak by 2×. A precision between two table entries is interpolated geometrically.

Memory-bandwidth-bound latency

Weights amortize once per step; KV reads scale with the group batch (§4):

tmem​(B)=BWmem​Tθ,device​+Bg​⋅TKV,token​​

This is the single-tier, dropped-α shorthand of the multi-tier α–β form in §4 — kept here for compactness on the assumption that on-die tier α contributes well under 0.1% of tmem​. Reinstate αi​ per §4 when modeling small-read regimes.

Sustained vs nameplate BWmem​. The system spec stores HBM bandwidth at the nameplate / datasheet value (e.g., 8 TB/s for HBM3e on B200, 4.8 TB/s for HBM3 on H200). Real production stacks sustain only a fraction of this peak: the dominant losses are bank conflicts under concurrent address streams (KV reads from many sequences hitting the same row), memory-controller queue depth, and competition between weight reads and KV-page-table gathers. Reported anchors across HBM generations and decode workloads:

Hardware (HBM gen)Sustained / nameplate BWmem​Notes
H100 / H200 (HBM3)~0.55Older memory controllers; sustained around 2.6 TB/s on H200’s nameplate 4.8 TB/s.
B200 / GB200 (HBM3e)0.7–1.0Better controllers + Blackwell command processor; the upper end (1.0) holds for software stacks that fuse aggressively on MoE workloads where access patterns are friendly; the lower end (0.7) for less-fused stacks on dense models.
B300 / GB300 (HBM3e)similar to B200Same memory subsystem class.
Dense models on minimally-fused runtimesas low as 0.4Worst-case observed on dense 70B-class models. Dense general matrix multiply (GEMM) sustains less of peak than MoE expert hopping on Blackwell — counter-intuitive but consistent with B200 production reports.

The right derate depends jointly on the chip, the model class, and the software stack — not on the chip alone — so it belongs in the calibration layer (a per-tier deflator on the device spec, or a single-tier override at analysis time) rather than baked into the device spec as a fixed property.

B-dependent sustained bandwidth ηβ​(B)

A constant ηβ​ captures the average sustained / nameplate ratio for a given (chip, software stack) but understates a real effect: HBM sustained bandwidth degrades with the active-sequence count B. Three mechanisms drive this:

  • Bank conflicts grow with concurrent address streams. At small B the weight-load pattern is well-coalesced — every weight byte loaded once, in long contiguous bursts. As B grows, each step also reads B separate KV histories whose addresses are scattered across HBM banks (paged-attention block-table indirection); collisions on the same DRAM row reduce the row-buffer hit rate.
  • Memory-controller queue depth saturates. Each HBM stack has a finite queue of in-flight requests. At small B the queue is mostly weight reads; at large B the queue fills with KV reads competing for the same controllers, and per-request latency grows even as throughput plateaus.
  • PCIe metadata bandwidth crowds in. Paged-attention block-table updates and per-step scheduler decisions push small writes to GPU memory across PCIe between forward passes. At very large B this “noise” memory traffic eats into the HBM channels’ usable bandwidth.

Reported HBM3e numbers on production-style decode workloads with paged attention: ~92% of peak at low concurrency (B≤16), ~85% at moderate B (∼64), ~75% at production B (∼512), ~55% at very large B (∼4000). The decline is monotone but non-linear — fastest in the B∈[16,512] range, flattening above B≈4000.

Promoting ηβ​ to a function of B extends the per-step memory-bandwidth-bound latency to:

tmem​(B)=BWmem,nameplate​⋅ηβ​(Bg​)Tθ,device​+Bg​⋅TKV,token​​

The curve is read at the number of sequences the device actually serves in the pass, Bg​. When ηβ​≡1 the formula reduces to the constant-bandwidth form above. A practical specification is a piecewise-linear curve through a small set of anchor batch sizes; a representative anchor set for HBM3e on Blackwell-class production stacks:

ηβ​(B)∈{(1,0.92),(64,0.85),(512,0.75),(4096,0.55)}

with linear interpolation between adjacent anchors and clamping at the boundaries.

Composition. ηβ​(B) composes multiplicatively with any constant per-tier deflator ηβ,tier​ (sram.md §1.2) and with the static sustained / nameplate calibration described above: BWeff​(B)=BWnameplate​⋅ηβ,tier​⋅ηβ​(B). In practice the analyst selects one of these to carry the sustained-vs-peak gap rather than composing all of them — a single calibrated quantity is easier to reason about.

When the curve matters. For decode workloads with B≤1024 a constant ηβ​ is usually sufficient — one calibration point captures the dominant sustained-vs-peak gap. The B-dependent curve becomes load-bearing only when (a) decode runs in a genuinely tmem​-bound regime — dense models on small-replica server-class deployments, very long contexts, MoE deployments with cheap all-to-all (small expert parallelism (EP), small per-expert FLOPs) — and (b) B extends across more than ~1.5 decades so the BW-saturation curvature shows up against measured time per output token (TPOT). Workloads dominated by collective communication (large EP, MoE all-to-all (A2A) on multi-node fabrics) sit on a different bottleneck and are unaffected by ηβ​(B).

Roofline local latency

tlocal​(B)=max(ηTC​(Bg​)tcompute​(B)​,tmem​(B))

ηTC​∈(0,1] is the tensor-core efficiency of the device at the batch it processes: matrix-multiply hardware reaches its peak rate only once the batch dimension fills its tile, so a small batch computes below RGPU​. It is a property of the device, given as a curve over batch size, and equals 1 when no curve is given, which recovers the plain roofline of §4.

Collective communication latency

From §5.5, with each per-axis t∗​(B) carrying its own B scaling on the β-side and the per-layer TP cost tTPlayer​(B) encoding the attention-mode-dependent AR / AG split (§5.3):

tcomm​(B)≈PPL​(tTPlayer​(B)+nSP​tSP​(B))+PPLmoe​​(nEP​tEP​(B))+tPP​(B)

Note: EP collectives only apply to MoE layers (Lmoe​), while TP and SP collectives apply to all layers.

Unified Overlap Model

We introduce an overlap factor ρcomm​∈[0,1] representing the fraction of local compute/memory time that is successfully utilized to hide communication.

The effective per-stage HW time is the local time plus any unhidden communication:

tstage,hw​(B)=tlocal​(B)+max(0,tcomm​(B)−ρcomm​⋅tlocal​(B))

This is the GPU-side wall-clock cost of one pipeline stage processing one pass of B sequences — purely hardware-intrinsic (compute + memory + interconnect, after collective overlap), no scheduling or host-side overhead. §7 introduces the per-stage kernel-launch dispatch budget tstage,kernel​ (§7.1), assembles the per-step hardware window over all PP stages, evaluating this stage time at the microbatch a stage actually processes (§7.2), and adds the per-sequence serving overhead plus throughput (§7.3) to produce the user-observed step time tstep,user​.

Regimes:

  • ρcomm​=0 (No Overlap): tstage,hw​(B)=tlocal​(B)+tcomm​(B) Typical for naive implementations or strictly sequential dependencies.

  • ρcomm​=1 (Perfect Overlap Opportunity): tstage,hw​(B)=tlocal​(B)+max(0,tcomm​(B)−tlocal​(B))=max(tlocal​(B),tcomm​(B)) Achieved by highly optimized kernels (e.g., Ring Attention) where independent work exists.

  • 0<ρcomm​<1 (Partial Overlap): Models real-world overheads (synchronization barriers, partial dependency chains) that prevent utilizing the full local duration for hiding comms. Kernel-launch overhead is not part of ρcomm​ here — it is modeled separately as tstage,kernel​ with its own overlap factor ρkernel​ in §7.1.

Realistic ρcomm​ for decode is small. A single decode step traverses every layer once with a tight data-dependency chain — attention → TP all-reduce → MoE dispatch (A2A) → expert FFN → MoE combine (A2A) → norm → next layer — and each step processes one batch through the full stack. Unlike training (and unlike prefill, which is compute-bound and has long collective windows to hide behind GEMM tiles), decode has no microbatch rotation to pipeline communication behind compute when PP is small (the typical production case). The within-layer overlap opportunities are narrow: stream-concurrent expert dispatch within an MoE block (dispatch to expert i+1 overlaps with FFN of expert i), TP all-reduce overlapped with the post-projection layernorm, and next-step host-side preparation (sampling, KV append) overlapped with the current step’s tail. Aggressively fused MoE dispatch implementations claim to hide roughly half the A2A behind compute under favorable conditions; vanilla decode stacks see far less. The realistic decode range is ρcomm​≈0–0.3, with ρcomm​=0 a sensible default for any deployment without explicit dispatch fusion or stream-concurrent expert pipelining. The ρcomm​≈0.7–1.0 values familiar from training and prefill literature are not directly applicable here.

LM head latency (stage PP-1 only)

The LM head H→V projection is a per-step one-shot kernel that fires only on the last PP stage. Its FLOPs (2Bg​HV/Demb​, §3.5) and weight + output traffic (TLM,θ,device​=HVb/Demb​ from §2.1, plus output activations Bg​⋅V⋅bact​, one logit row per sequence the device’s group serves) define a small standalone roofline:

tLM,hw​(B)=max(RGPU​2Bg​HV/Demb​​,BWmem​HVb/Demb​+Bg​Vbact​​)

Because the LM head lives on stage PP−1 only (not divided by PP or SP), it is bookkept as a separate additive term rather than folded into the per-layer tlocal​(B). §7.2 adds it once per token, after the PP stage passes.

6.3 When Each Layout / Attention-Mode Pays

§6.1 and §6.2 cover what each combination of layout and attention mode costs in HBM and per-step latency. This subsection covers which configuration to pick for a given deployment — when each of the four production-relevant configurations of §1.4 actually pays off relative to the orthogonal + TP-attention default.

Orthogonal + TP-attention (the default)

The legacy Megatron-LM partition: every linear layer is TP-sharded by head, KV cache is head-sharded by TP, the per-layer attention block fires an all-reduce. Use this when:

  • Multi-head attention (MHA) or grouped-query attention (GQA) with non-trivial Hkv​, where attention parameters are 8–15% of model size and replicating them on every TP rank would meaningfully inflate the per-device memory budget.
  • Small GTP​ on a single fast fabric tier (e.g., TP≤8 on NVLink), where the per-attention all-reduce is small enough that the AR → AG savings in DP-attention are second-order.
  • Mixed dense + MoE architectures where the attention block’s TP shard is meaningful relative to the dense FFN’s TP shard.

Orthogonal + DP-attention

Replicates attention weights on every TP rank; replaces the per-layer attention all-reduce with an all-gather (half the cost). The trade is one-attention-AR-per-layer saved against TP−1 extra copies of the attention weights in HBM and one extra all-reduce-equivalent of attention weight memory traffic per step. Favorable when:

  1. Attention parameters are a small fraction of model size. Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA, DSv3) shrinks Hkv​ from ∼H in MHA down to ∼H/14, dropping attention parameters from ∼15% of the model to ∼3%. Replicating 3% of the weights costs little; saving an all-reduce per layer is worth a lot when there are 60+ layers and the all-reduce sits on the critical path. [DSV3, SGLANG-DPATTN]
  2. GTP​ is large enough that GTP​−1 all-reduces of B⋅Hb payload per stage dominate the latency budget. At GTP​=8 on NVLink the savings are second-order; at GTP​=32 on a multi-node setup they become first-order.
  3. Memory-bound regime (B small relative to crossover B⋆ from §4). Here the extra attention weight traffic adds at most GTP​GTP​−1​⋅Mθ,device, TP-attn​Mattn, TP-attn​​ to the per-step weight traffic — for an MLA-class model with attention parameters at ∼3% of total weights and GTP​=8, that is a ~2.6% increase in tmem​. The per-layer AR savings typically dwarf this term, so the trade is favorable; in compute-bound regime the trade is closer to neutral because attention compute is invariant under the swap.

For models with full MHA or GQA where attention parameters are 8–15% of total weight, the calculus is closer; for models with MLA the trade essentially always favors DP-attention.

Co-located + DP-attention

TP and EP overlap on the same physical GPUs of a replica, dropping Nreplica​ from PP⋅TP⋅EP⋅SP to PP⋅max(TP,EP)⋅SP. With both axes inside one NVLink island, both the TP collective and the EP all-to-all stay on the fastest fabric tier. The catch: each device now holds 1/EP of the experts (no further TP shard within an expert), which inflates per-device expert memory by a factor of TP relative to the orthogonal layout. Favorable when:

  1. Per-device HBM can absorb the larger expert footprint. Either the expert weights are small enough (low Nexp​ or compact Imoe​) or aggressive quantization (FP4 / INT4) keeps 1/EP of the experts under HBM. DSv3 satisfies this via FP4 + a sparsity factor of k=8 active experts out of Nexp​=256. [DSV3]
  2. All collectives benefit from staying inside one fast fabric tier. Orthogonal TP=8,EP=8 on 64 GPUs spans multiple NVLink islands — the EP all-to-all crosses a slower tier on every layer, paying the slow tier’s α on every collective. Co-located TP=EP=8 on 8 GPUs keeps both collectives on NVLink. The latency win is concentrated in the small-M decode regime where α dominates.
  3. Attention mode choice under co-location. Co-location supports both attention modes on the overlaid GPU set: TP-attn head-shards across the same group that holds the experts (no replication cost; per-layer TP all-reduce fires on the same ranks as the MoE A2A), and DP-attn replicates attention and batch-shards (replication cost equal to orthogonal + DP-attn — fine for MLA / aggressive GQA models, costly for full MHA). Pick TP-attn under co-location when the attention block is head-structured enough to benefit from sharding (nq​ divides TP, GQA nkv​≥TP, or full MHA); pick DP-attn when MLA flatness or aggressive-GQA nkv​ saturation makes attention replication free anyway.

In short: co-location is the right choice when the workload is MoE-dominated, attention is small (MLA-class), and keeping the world inside one NVLink island unlocks meaningful α-cost savings on every collective.

Quick decision table

SymptomRecommended configuration
Dense or small-MoE model, MHA/GQA attention, GTP​≤8orthogonal + TP-attn (the default)
MLA-class attention, single fabric tier, GTP​≤8orthogonal + DP-attn
MLA-class attention, large GTP​ on multi-tier fabricorthogonal + DP-attn
MLA-class attention, MoE-dominant, TP=EP targets a single NVLink islandco-located + DP-attn
MoE-dominant, head-structured attention (MHA / GQA with nkv​≥TP), TP=EP overlaid on the same NVLink islandco-located + TP-attn (the DeepSeek-R1 single-rack NVL72 pattern)
Multi-tier fabric where orthogonal would put EP A2A on slower tierco-located + DP-attn (when memory permits)

7. Host-Side Overheads and Throughput

§6.2 produced tstage,hw​(B) (per-stage body) and tLM,hw​(B) (one-shot LM head on stage PP−1) — the hardware-intrinsic per-pass time pieces, the lower bound set by tensor-core compute, HBM bandwidth, and on-/off-chip interconnect. Two facts about autoregressive decode decide how they combine (§7.2 derives both):

  • Every token pays the whole pipeline. A sequence’s next token cannot enter the first stage until its previous token has left the last one, so the time between two tokens of a sequence is the traversal PP⋅tstage,hw​(Bmb​)+tLM,hw​(Bmb​) — one stage pass on each of the PP stages, then the LM head — and never the time of a single stage. This holds for every decode step, not only for the first token. There is no steady state in which a sequence emits one token per stage time: that schedule belongs to training, where successive microbatches are independent of one another.
  • A stage processes a microbatch, not the batch. The B in-flight sequences circulate through the stages as microbatches of Bmb​=max(1,B/PP) sequences, and every per-stage quantity of §2–§6 is evaluated at Bmb​. What pipeline depth buys is concurrency, not a shorter path: the PP stages work on different microbatches at the same time, so the replica still delivers B tokens per traversal. This is the quantity that drives TPS in §7.3.

The first token of a request is produced by the prefill pass, whose time is the main hardware contribution to time to first token (TTFT); it is derived in the companion prefill document, which is not a chapter of this book.

A real serving step does not run at this lower bound. Three things turn tstage,hw​ into the user-observed step time — the first and third are host-side overheads (CPU work and command-processor dispatch sitting outside the GPU pipeline), the second is the pipeline traversal just described:

  1. Kernel-launch overhead (per microbatch, ~constant in B) — the host-side dispatch budget for the layer + collective + PP-hop kernels that fire each microbatch. Each kernel launch pays a fixed τlaunch​ regardless of payload size, so the term scales with kernel count, not with B. Whether it is hidden by GPU work or surfaces as a hard floor depends on async dispatch overlap. §7.1 derives this as tstage,kernel​ in the same per-step per-stage units as tstage,hw​.
  2. Pipeline traversal — a token crosses all PP stages, so the per-stage body cost is paid PP times per token, at the microbatch size Bmb​=max(1,B/PP) that one stage processes per pass (of which one device group handles Bg​(Bmb​)=max(1,Bmb​/Dbatch​), §1.4). The factor PP is a global multiplier on whatever per-stage body cost dominates, so it sits outside the per-axis composition rather than as a per-axis correction.
  3. Per-sequence serving runtime overhead (per sequence, linear in B) — host-side bookkeeping the runtime must perform once per active sequence per step: PagedAttention block-table assembly, continuous-batching scheduler decisions, sampling glue, token-append. The term scales as O(B) and sits on the critical path of every step (it cannot overlap with GPU work in eager mode; under CUDA-Graph replay it hides behind the per-step GPU window until it overflows). §7.3 derives this as tstep,seq​(B) and assembles the full tstep,user​(B) on top of §7.2’s per-step hardware window.

The two host-side overheads are distinct in three ways: scaling with B (constant vs linear), where the cost is paid (per microbatch dispatch vs once-per-step head-node bookkeeping), and whether they can overlap with GPU work (yes, partially, for kernel-launch via CUDA Graphs / async pipelining; partially under CUDA-Graph replay for serving runtime, zero overlap in eager-mode stacks). §7.2 assembles tstage,hw​, tstage,kernel​, the PP-stage traversal, and tLM,hw​ into the per-step hardware window tstep,base​(B); §7.3 adds tstep,seq​(B) on top to recover the user-observed step time tstep,user​(B) and derives the throughput metrics TPS / TTPS.

7.1 Kernel-launch overhead

The user-observed step time also includes a dispatch budget tstage,kernel​ — the cost of getting one microbatch’s worth of kernels onto the GPU on this stage. Where that cost is paid depends on the execution mode: in eager mode it is literal CPU cudaLaunchKernel latency on the host side (τlaunch​≈7μs); under CUDA Graphs / DAG replay the host issues a single cudaGraphLaunch per microbatch and the per-node work shifts to the GPU’s command processor walking the captured DAG (τlaunch​≈1.5μs, dominated by command-buffer overhead, not CPU API time). The model collapses both regimes into a single per-kernel launch time τlaunch​, and the name “kernel-launch overhead” applies to both paths. τlaunch​ is a property of the serving stack: it belongs to the description of the software that runs the model, together with the kernel counts and the overlap factor below, and not to the workload or to the device. The two figures above are what the mechanism alone predicts. The values used per stack are effective ones, which also absorb kernels that the captured graph does not cover and kernel counts above the flat per-layer count assumed here: 1.5 µs for a compiled runtime on full graph replay, 4 µs for the same runtime under a serving orchestrator, 8 and 12 µs for interpreter-based runtimes under an orchestrator, and 10 µs for interpreter-driven stacks on their own. framework.md §4 lists them per stack and says which are calibrated against measurement and which are starting points.

tstage,kernel​ is per microbatch, per stage — same units as tstage,hw​ (§6.2), so the two compose directly in §7.2 without a unit mismatch. EP launches only fire on the Lmoe​/PP MoE layers this stage owns (mirroring the Lmoe​/PP factor in §5.5’s tcomm​ formula); for a pure dense model Lmoe​=0 and the EP term vanishes.

tstage,kernel​=τlaunch​⋅[PPL​(kcompute​+kcollective​(nTP​+nSP​))+PPLmoe​​⋅kcollective​⋅nEP​+kpp_hop​]

What kcompute​ counts. kcompute​ is the number of non-NCCL compute kernels fired per layer — GEMMs, attention, layernorms, activations, residuals. With a fused stack (FlashAttention + Megatron-style fused MLP) a decode layer fires roughly: (1) fused QKV projection, (2) FlashAttention forward, (3) output projection, (4) fused residual + post-attention norm, (5) fused gate + up + activation, (6) down projection, (7) residual. ~8–12 launches in production; default is 10. Aggressive ahead-of-time compilation (e.g. TensorRT engine) drops this to 3–5; eager-mode PyTorch without fusion can push it to 30+. Tighter compilation reduces kcompute​; CUDA Graphs reduce τlaunch​ — these are independent levers and production stacks generally use both.

Per-layer accounting — two nested layers for collectives. nTP​,nEP​,nSP​ from §5.5 count NCCL API calls per layer (logical operations: e.g. nTP​=2 means “two ncclAllReduce calls per layer — one in attn, one in MLP”). The tcomm​ formula in §5.5 prices each call once via n∗​⋅t∗​. The launch counter goes one level deeper: each NCCL API call internally fires kcollective​ separate cudaLaunchKernel events (default 2 — typically a setup/coordination kernel plus the reduction kernel), so the total kernel launches per layer per axis is n∗​⋅kcollective​. That product is what τlaunch​ is paid for. Custom collectives that fuse the call into a single kernel set kcollective​=1; multi-kernel implementations may set it higher. Each n∗​ is zeroed when the corresponding axis size is 1 (the collective never fires).

Three additive contributions in the bracket: (1) compute + TP + SP launches on every layer this stage owns (L/PP layers); (2) EP launches on MoE layers only (Lmoe​/PP layers); (3) one P2P transit (default kpp_hop​=2: 1 recv + 1 send on a middle stage; edge stages do only one direction, off by half a launch — negligible at PP>1). The PP-hop term is inert when PP=1.

tstage,kernel​ is composed with the GPU-side tstage,hw​ via the kernel-launch overlap factor ρkernel​∈[0,1] — at ρkernel​=1 (the production default for CUDA-Graphs-replayed serving), async dispatch fully overlaps with GPU work and tstage,kernel​ acts as a floor that only kicks in when the per-microbatch launch budget exceeds tstage,hw​; at ρkernel​=0, dispatch is synchronous and the costs add linearly. Intermediate values are in use as well: 0.3 for the two interpreter-driven stacks, whose interpreter stalls keep the host from running ahead of the GPU, and values fitted per measured setup between 0.35 and 0.85 for an orchestrated compiled runtime (framework.md §4). Setting τlaunch​=0 removes tstage,kernel​ entirely (the plain roofline).

The tensor-core efficiency ηTC​ of §6.2 is a separate matter. It derates the compute roofline at small batch and is a property of the device, part of the hardware description beside the peak compute rate and the memory bandwidth, not of the serving stack; when the device gives no curve it is 1 and the term is a no-op.

7.2 Per-step hardware window

Building on the kernel-launch dispatch budget tstage,kernel​ from §7.1 and the per-stage hardware body tstage,hw​ from §6.2, we assemble the per-step hardware window tstep,base​(B) — the hardware-side time between two consecutive tokens of one sequence, covering its traversal of all PP pipeline stages and the LM head after the last one. When the serving runtime adds no host-side per-sequence work (the host-overhead-free roofline), the user-observed step time equals tstep,base​(B). §7.3 then adds the per-sequence serving overhead on top of tstep,base​(B) to recover the full tstep,user​(B) and derives throughput from it.

How the pipeline carries autoregressive decode

Pipeline parallelism splits the model’s L layers into PP contiguous stages, each owned by a different device (or device group). A token cannot skip stages — it is transformed by stage 0, then forwarded to stage 1, and so on through stage PP−1 before its logits are produced.

Decode adds a constraint that training and prefill do not have: a sequence’s next token cannot enter stage 0 until its previous token has left stage PP−1 and been sampled. A sequence therefore occupies exactly one stage at a time, and the time between two of its tokens is the full traversal of the pipeline, never the time of a single stage. This is the difference from the training schedules of [MEGATRON3], where successive microbatches are independent and one result emerges per stage time once the pipeline has filled.

What the pipeline can do is work on different sequences in different stages. The B in-flight sequences are split into microbatches that circulate through the stages one behind another: while stage 0 processes one microbatch, stage 1 processes the one ahead of it, and so on. Two regimes follow:

  • Pipeline full (B≥PP). There are PP microbatches of B/PP sequences each, and every stage is busy all the time.
  • Pipeline underfilled (B<PP). There are only B microbatches of one sequence each, and PP−B stages are idle at any instant.

Both are captured by the microbatch size, the number of sequences one stage processes in one pass:

Bmb​=max(1,PPB​)

Every per-stage quantity of §2–§6 is a function of the batch a stage processes in one pass. With PP>1 that batch is Bmb​, not B: the stage computes Bmb​ tokens, reads the KV history of Bmb​ sequences, its collectives carry Bmb​ tokens of activations, and the MoE touched-expert fraction (§2.1) is that of a batch of Bmb​. The per-stage hardware time that enters the step is therefore tstage,hw​(Bmb​). At PP=1, Bmb​=B and nothing changes.

The microbatch composes with the batch divisor of §1.4. Under the orthogonal layout the stage is itself EP device groups, and the microbatch is spread over them: one device handles Bg​(Bmb​)=max(1,Bmb​/Dbatch​) sequences per pass for attention, the dense FFN, the router, the KV read, the collective payloads and the LM head, while the expert FFN sees all Bmb​ tokens. The two divisions are independent: PP divides the batch in time (which microbatch a stage is working on), Dbatch​ divides it in space (which group of the stage holds a sequence). Memory capacity is the exception to the first: every stage holds its layers’ share of the cache of all B resident sequences, so the footprint of §1.4 is counted at Bg​(B), not at Bg​(Bmb​).

Step time

A token pays one stage pass on each of the PP stages, then the LM head. Composing tstage,hw​ (§6.2) and tstage,kernel​ (§7.1) on each stage follows the same overlap pattern as the compute/comm overlap in §6.2 — hardware work runs as the base, host dispatch overlaps for a fraction ρkernel​ of it, and any unhidden remainder serializes after:

tstep,base​(B)=PP⋅[tstage,hw​(Bmb​)+max(0,tstage,kernel​−ρkernel​⋅tstage,hw​(Bmb​))]+tLM,hw​(Bmb​)

The factor PP assumes uniform stages (all PP stages have identical body cost). The LM head tLM,hw​ from §6.2 is added once: a token passes it once, after the last stage. Treating it as an additive term rather than as a bottleneck on stage PP−1 assumes the layer split is balanced so that the last stage’s body plus the LM head matches the other stages’ bodies; an unbalanced split would instead pace every stage to the slowest one.

Regimes (assuming ρkernel​=1, the production CUDA-Graph default):

  • tstage,hw​(Bmb​)≥tstage,kernel​: the overflow term is 0 and the body is hardware-bound — async dispatch is fully hidden by hardware work. This is the typical regime for moderate-to-large B on production stacks.
  • tstage,hw​(Bmb​)<tstage,kernel​: the kernel-launch budget surfaces as a floor on every stage, so the step time is PP⋅tstage,kernel​ — the launch budget of all L layers plus the inter-stage hops, whatever the depth of the pipeline (common at small B on dense decode).
  • ρkernel​=0: no overlap — kernel-launch dispatch serializes additively after GPU compute on every stage. Eager-mode stacks land here.

What pipeline depth buys

Substituting the memory-bound stage time shows what PP does and does not change. A stage holds 1/PP of the layers, so it reads 1/PP of the weights and 1/PP of each sequence’s KV history per pass; over the PP passes of one traversal these sum back to the whole model. With Tθ​ and TKV,token​ the per-pass traffic at PP=1 (written for one device group; with Dbatch​>1 read Bg​(Bmb​) for Bmb​):

PP⋅tstage,hw​(Bmb​)≈BWmem​Tθ​+Bmb​⋅TKV,token​​

The weight term is independent of PP: every token still reads every weight once. Only the KV term shrinks, because a traversal now carries B/PP sequences instead of B. The compute and collective terms behave the same way (their payloads scale with Bmb​), and the collective startup latencies and the kernel-launch floor, which are per layer, do not shrink at all. Pipeline depth therefore does not shorten a token’s path through the model. It buys two other things: each device holds 1/PP of the weights and of the KV cache, which lets a model fit and lets a replica admit a larger batch; and the PP stages serve PP microbatches concurrently, which raises the throughput of a replica that now occupies PP times the devices. Whether throughput per device rises depends on whether the larger admissible batch outweighs that device count.

At B=1 the step is PP⋅tstage,hw​(1) plus the LM head — the same traversal as the non-pipelined model, with PP−1 of the stages idle at any instant.

tstep,base​(B) is the full per-step hardware window — the time the host can use to hide per-sequence serving work behind GPU compute. At B=1,PP=1 with tstage,kernel​=0, it reduces to tstage,hw​(1)+tLM,hw​(1) — single-stage body plus LM head, the non-pipelined decode model with a vocab projection at the end.

When the serving runtime contributes no per-sequence host work (cseq​=0, see §7.3), the user-observed step time equals the hardware window: tstep,user​(B)=tstep,base​(B). The general case adds the per-sequence serving overhead on top — derived in §7.3.

7.3 Per-sequence serving runtime overhead and throughput

§7.1 captured the per-microbatch kernel-launch dispatch budget, and §7.2 assembled the per-step hardware window tstep,base​(B) from it. A separate class of host-side overhead is per active sequence rather than per microbatch: work the runtime must perform once for each of the B in-flight sequences on every decode step, regardless of payload size. Production inference serving stacks (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, NVIDIA Dynamo) all incur this overhead [VLLM, ORCA, DYNAMO]; four components dominate it:

  • Block-table gather and metadata marshaling. PagedAttention stores each sequence’s key-value (KV) cache as a list of fixed-size blocks; on every step the runtime assembles the per-sequence block table (one indirection per active sequence) and ships it to the attention kernel as a metadata buffer. The per-sequence cost is small but unavoidable, and the total scales as O(B).
  • Continuous-batching scheduler decisions. Iteration-level scheduling (the ORCA / vLLM design [ORCA]) re-evaluates the active set on every step: admit any newly arrived request that fits, evict any sequence that just finished, decide whether prefills can piggyback this step. The decision logic is per-sequence and runs on the CPU between two consecutive forward passes.
  • Per-sequence sampling glue. Greedy / top-k / top-p / multinomial sampling runs one decision per sequence per step. The logits-softmax-then-sample kernel itself is GPU-side and is absorbed into tLM,hw​(B), but the host wraps each sampling decision in per-sequence Python / C++ glue (penalty application, stop-token checks, output-token append, end-of-sequence (EOS) / stop-string detection) that is genuinely O(B) on the CPU.
  • Token-append and KV-write bookkeeping. Append the newly sampled token to the per-sequence output buffer, advance the per-sequence position counter, allocate a new block on overflow, write the block-table update — one bookkeeping pass per active sequence per step.

Alongside these four per-sequence components, every decode step incurs a B-independent orchestration floor that fires once per step regardless of how many sequences are active:

  • Per-step orchestration. CUDA-Graph launch decision logic, scheduler tick (active-set advance, time-budget accounting), output framing (response-stream multiplexing for streaming responses), KV block-table refresh metadata, and any Python sampler / scheduler glue that runs between graph replays rather than per-sequence. These costs survive CUDA-Graph absorption — the graph captures the GPU kernel sequence but not the host-side decisions that fire between graph launches. Where a measured setup has been fitted, this floor is what closes the gap that remains at small batch once the per-sequence term has been fitted at large batch: the fitted values run from zero to a few milliseconds per step (framework.md §4).

This per-step host work is distinct from two other overheads tracked elsewhere:

  • The kernel-launch dispatch budget tstage,kernel​ from §7.1 is per microbatch per stage and is essentially independent of B. Each NCCL or cudaLaunchKernel event fires once per layer regardless of the per-call payload; the per-event cost models GPU-command-processor latency or eager-mode CPU API time, not host-side per-step orchestration.
  • The per-request scheduler latency tsched​ tracked in framework.md §1 fires once per request when the request enters the system, not on every decode step. The bookkeeping captured here is the recurring delta on top of tsched​ that fires every step the request remains active.

The aggregate per-step gross host cost combines the B-independent orchestration floor corch​ with the per-sequence linear term cseq​⋅B:

tstep,seq​(B)=corch​+cseq​⋅B

with units of seconds per step (both constants are quoted in microseconds below). corch​ captures the once-per-step orchestration work; cseq​ captures the per-sequence inner loops. B here is the replica’s whole in-flight batch, not the microbatch: the host does this work once per sequence per token whatever the pipeline depth. With corch​=cseq​=0 the term vanishes and the step is the host-overhead-free roofline; both constants belong to the description of the serving stack.

Composition with the hardware window. Like tstage,kernel​ (§7.1), the per-sequence serving work admits a CUDA-Graph-replay overlap: under graph replay the CPU launches the per-step graph in ∼1.5 µs and is then free for the duration of the hardware step window tstep,base​(B) (§7.2), which it uses for exactly this per-sequence work (block-table assembly for the next step, sampling glue for the previous step’s outputs, scheduler bookkeeping). The host work hides behind the hardware window until tstep,seq​(B) exceeds tstep,base​(B), at which point only the excess blocks. The composition is parameterized by an overlap factor ρseq​∈[0,1], applied to the per-step hardware window from §7.2:

tstep,user​(B)=tstep,base​(B)+max(0,tstep,seq​(B)−ρseq​⋅tstep,base​(B))

with ρseq​=1 for CUDA-Graph-replay stacks (full overlap; default), ρseq​=0 for eager-mode stacks where Python interpreter stalls between graph launches break the CPU-runs-ahead invariant (host work always blocks). The two regimes are:

  • CUDA-Graph regime (ρseq​=1). When tstep,seq​(B)≤tstep,base​(B), the overflow is 0 and tstep,user​(B)=tstep,base​(B) — host work is fully hidden. When tstep,seq​(B)>tstep,base​(B), only the excess blocks the next step’s hardware window.
  • Eager regime (ρseq​=0). The overflow becomes the full tstep,seq​(B) — the Python interpreter cannot use the GPU compute window for the next step’s setup, so host work serializes after GPU compute.

The serving term sits outside the PP-stage traversal since it fires once per step on the head node regardless of how the body is pipelined across stages — the traversal is already absorbed inside tstep,base​(B) from §7.2. This composition is identical in form to tstage,kernel​’s composition via ρkernel​ (§7.1); the two terms model different host-side work (per-microbatch dispatch vs per-sequence runtime) but admit the same overlap physics.

When cseq​=0, tstep,user​(B)=tstep,base​(B) — the user-observed step time collapses to the hardware-only roofline derived in §7.2. When tstage,kernel​=0 as well (host-overhead-free), the formula reduces all the way to tstage,hw​(B)+tLM,hw​(B) at PP=1.

Stack-dependent calibration. cseq​ captures the constant factor in the per-sequence inner loop, which differs across serving frameworks (interpreter-heavy vs compiled and graph-replayed), runtime configurations (eager mode vs CUDA Graphs, interpreted sampling vs fused-CUDA sampling), and paged-attention block sizes. Two kinds of number must be kept apart: the range reported for a class of stack, and the single value the model uses for a named stack until a measurement of the setup at hand replaces it. The table gives both, and says which values rest on measurement.

StackReported range of cseq​Value used: cseq​, ρseq​Status
Compiled runtime under a serving orchestrator (NVIDIA Dynamo wrapping TensorRT-LLM)5–22 µs/seq5 µs/seq, ρseq​=1Calibrated. The orchestrator absorbs most per-step bookkeeping into a single graph launch, leaving the irreducible per-sequence sampling and block-table work. Fits on three measured setups give 3.0–5.5 µs/seq.
Interpreter-based runtime under the same orchestrator (NVIDIA Dynamo wrapping SGLang)not separately reported5 µs/seq, ρseq​=1Carried over from the row above, on the argument that the orchestrator’s absorption of per-sequence work does not depend on the runtime it wraps; compared with one measured setup, not fitted to it. An earlier version of this table gave 25–50 µs/seq for this stack; the model does not use that figure. What differs from the row above is the kernel-launch time (§7.1).
Second interpreter-based runtime under the same orchestrator (NVIDIA Dynamo wrapping vLLM)not separately reported5 µs/seq, ρseq​=1Unmeasured starting point, assumed equal to the two rows above.
Raw compiled runtime, no orchestrator (TensorRT-LLM)50–100 µs/seq75 µs/seq, ρseq​=1Starting point (middle of the range). Fits on three measured setups give 49–85 µs/seq, together with a per-step floor corch​ of 1.25–4.15 ms and ρseq​=0.
