KV Cache Management: Paging, Fragmentation, and Traffic Overhead

Author: Yue Lu
Date: April 2026

Keywords:
KV cache, PagedAttention, block allocation, fragmentation, HBM capacity, memory management, LLM inference, paged memory, beam search, copy-on-write, sequence parallelism

Abstract

The baseline key-value (KV) cache model in decode.md §1.3 and §2.3 assumes contiguous allocation: keys and values for all S token positions are stored and accessed as a single dense tensor per layer. Real production serving systems, however, use paged KV allocation (PagedAttention [VLLM]) to enable dynamic memory sharing, efficient preemption, and fine-grained capacity management. Paging introduces internal fragmentation — the last block of each sequence is typically partially filled — and additional traffic overhead for block-table lookups, copy-on-write branching, and potential preemption events. This document quantifies the fragmentation overhead analytically, sizes the other three and states which of them the model evaluates (block-table lookups are dropped as negligible; copy-on-write and preemption are not modelled), derives a fragmentation-corrected HBM capacity model, and shows how paging interacts with tensor-parallel (TP), sequence-parallel (SP), and pipeline-parallel (PP) sharding.

Table of Contents

  • 1. Baseline KV Model (from decode.md)
  • 2. PagedAttention Block Structure
  • 3. Fragmentation Factor
    • 3.1 Internal Fragmentation
    • 3.2 External Fragmentation
  • 4. Block Allocation Traffic Overhead
    • 4.1 Block Table Lookup
    • 4.2 Copy-on-Write for Beam Search and Parallel Sampling
    • 4.3 Preemption and Recompute
  • 5. Interaction with TP and SP Sharding
  • 6. Effective HBM Capacity Model

Scope: The formulas in this document are written for a standard grouped-query or multi-query attention (GQA / MQA) cache, which stores 2Hkv​ elements per token per layer with Hkv​=nkv​⋅dhead​. Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), as used in DeepSeek-V2/V3, is modelled, by two substitutions that apply to every formula below. First, the per-token-per-layer cache is the head-shared latent, (dc​+dqk,rope​) elements, in place of 2Hkv​ (attention.md §3.4). Second, the latent is not head-structured, so under TP-attention it cannot be split across the TP ranks: every rank holds the whole latent and the KV divisor Dkv​ defined in §1 is replaced by 1 (attention.md §3.6); under DP-attention Dkv​ applies as written. The paging arithmetic (blocks, fragmentation, capacity) is otherwise unchanged.

1. Baseline KV Model (from decode.md)

This section briefly restates the contiguous KV model established in decode.md §1.3 and §2.3 as the reference point. The derivations are not repeated here; refer to those sections for the full treatment.

Per-layer KV memory (§1.3)

For a single attention layer with a context of S tokens and KV projection dimension Hkv​ (with Hkv​=nkv​⋅dhead​, per [GQA]):

MKV,layer​=2SHkv​b

where the factor of 2 accounts for both keys and values, and b is bytes per element.

Per-device KV memory after sharding (§1.4)

Under pipeline parallelism (PP), tensor parallelism (TP), and sequence parallelism (SP), each device owns L/PP layers, a 1/Dkv​ share of one sequence’s cache, and 1/SP of the sequence dimension. Dkv​ is the KV divisor of decode.md §1.4: the number of devices one sequence’s cache is divided across by head or by sequence, not counting SP. It equals TP when the TP and expert-parallel (EP) groups are disjoint device sets (the orthogonal layout), whether attention is head-sharded across the TP group (TP-attention) or the batch is split across it (DP-attention), and max(TP,EP) when TP and EP share the same devices (the co-located layout, which requires TP=EP). For one sequence:

MKV,token​=PPL​⋅Dkv​⋅SP2SHkv​b​

A device holds the caches of the sequences its own device group serves. Under the orthogonal layout a replica is EP groups of TP devices, each with its own copy of the attention weights and its own caches, so a batch of B sequences is spread over Dbatch​=EP groups; under the co-located layout, and for a dense model, there is one group and Dbatch​=1. Dbatch​ is the batch divisor of decode.md §1.4, and the number of sequences a device holds is the group batch Bg​=max(1,B/Dbatch​):

MKV,device​(B)=Bg​⋅MKV,token​

Per-device KV traffic per token (§2.3)

Each new generated token requires reading the full KV history of its sequence. Per device and per sequence:

TKV,token​≈PPL​⋅Dkv​⋅SP2SHkv​b​

and over the sequences the device serves in one stage pass, TKV,device​=Bg​⋅TKV,token​. FlashAttention does not reduce this term: history keys and values must always be loaded regardless of tiling strategy.

Assumption in the baseline: the expressions above treat KV storage as a contiguous dense tensor. The remainder of this document models the overhead introduced when that assumption is relaxed by paged allocation.

2. PagedAttention Block Structure

PagedAttention [VLLM] divides the KV cache into fixed-size blocks, each storing KV entries for BLKKV​ consecutive token positions. Blocks are allocated from a shared pool and may be physically non-contiguous; a per-sequence block table maps logical block indices to physical addresses.

Block size and per-block storage

Each block stores keys and values for BLKKV​ token positions across all L/PP layers on the device, sharded by the KV divisor Dkv​ of §1 and by SP. The per-block KV footprint is:

Mblock​=BLKKV​⋅Dkv​⋅SP2Hkv​b⋅(L/PP)​

This is the granularity at which memory is allocated and freed. For an MLA model the numerator carries the latent (dc​+dqk,rope​) in place of 2Hkv​, and under TP-attention the divisor is SP alone (see the scope note).

Convention note: This document defines a KV block at the device level, spanning all L/PP layers on the device. vLLM’s implementation allocates blocks per-layer (each block stores BLKKV​ tokens for one layer). The two conventions yield identical total memory; the device-level block simplifies the fragmentation and capacity analysis below.

Blocks required per sequence

A logical sequence of S tokens requires:

Nblocks​(S)=⌈BLKKV​S​⌉

blocks. The last block is filled with SmodBLKKV​ tokens; if this is non-zero, the remainder of the block is reserved but unused — the source of internal fragmentation.

Symbol definitions

SymbolDefinition
BLKKV​KV block size in tokens (typical: 16 or 32)
Nblocks​(S)Blocks allocated for a sequence of length S: ⌈S/BLKKV​⌉
φFragmentation factor: ratio of allocated KV memory to ideally occupied KV memory
MHBM,KV,avail​HBM capacity available for KV storage after weights and activations
Smax​Maximum supportable context length given MHBM,KV,avail​ and φ

3. Fragmentation Factor

3.1 Internal Fragmentation

The last block of each sequence is on average half-full for a uniform distribution of sequence lengths relative to block size. More precisely, the expected number of wasted token slots per sequence is:

E[wasted tokens]=2BLKKV​−1​≈2BLKKV​​

We define the fragmentation factor φ as the ratio of allocated capacity to logically occupied capacity:

φ(S)=SNblocks​(S)⋅BLKKV​​=S⌈S/BLKKV​⌉⋅BLKKV​​

Boundary behavior:

  • S≫BLKKV​: φ→1 — fragmentation is negligible for long contexts.
  • S=BLKKV​: φ=1 — exactly one full block, no waste.
  • S=1: φ=BLKKV​ — worst case, one entire block reserved for a single token.

For uniform sequence-length distribution over [1,Smax​], the expectation of φ simplifies to a first-order approximation:

φavg​≈1+2SBLKKV​​

This approximation holds when S≫BLKKV​/2, which is satisfied for all realistic serving workloads (e.g., S≥512, BLKKV​≤32).

Practical implication: for BLKKV​=16 and S=4096, φavg​≈1+16/(2⋅4096)≈1.002, i.e., less than 0.2% overhead. For S=64, φavg​≈1.125, i.e., 12.5% overhead — a meaningful penalty at short contexts.

3.2 External Fragmentation

External fragmentation arises when freed blocks cannot be coalesced into large enough contiguous regions for new allocations. Because PagedAttention allocates and frees at fixed block granularity (blocks are interchangeable), external fragmentation is structurally zero for LLM serving: any free block can satisfy any allocation request. This is a deliberate design property of [VLLM].

The one exception is systems that require physically contiguous multi-block regions (e.g., for hardware DMA or non-paged attention kernels); this case is outside the scope of the analytical model here.

4. Block Allocation Traffic Overhead

The baseline KV traffic TKV,device​ from decode.md §2.3 accounts for reading and writing KV tensor values. Paged allocation introduces additional memory operations beyond this: block-table lookups, copy-on-write for branching, and preemption. None of the three is a term of the model: the first is negligible, and the other two are outside what the model evaluates. Each subsection says which.

4.1 Block Table Lookup

Each attention kernel invocation must resolve the physical address of each block via the block table before accessing KV values. For a sequence of length S:

  • Block table has Nblocks​(S)=⌈S/BLKKV​⌉ entries, each a pointer (typically 4 or 8 bytes).
  • Total block table traffic per sequence per layer: ⌈S/BLKKV​⌉⋅pptr​ bytes, where pptr​∈{4,8}.

For BLKKV​=16, S=4096, and pptr​=8: block table traffic is 256×8=2048 bytes per layer, versus 2×4096×128×2≈2 MB of KV values. The ratio is approximately 0.05% — negligible for all practical configurations.

Modeling decision: block table lookup traffic is omitted from the analytical traffic model.

4.2 Copy-on-Write for Beam Search and Parallel Sampling

When a sequence branches (e.g., beam search with width W, or parallel sampling), PagedAttention defers physical copying using a copy-on-write (CoW) mechanism [VLLM]: shared blocks are reference-counted and copied only when a branch writes a new token that would modify a shared block.

What is modelled. The model prices independent sequences: every sequence in the batch owns all of its blocks and reads its own history, which is greedy decode or independent sampling. For that case there is no shared block and the copy-on-write traffic is zero, so TKV,device​ from the baseline model is exact:

TCoW​=0

What is not modelled. The beam width W is not an input the model evaluates. Neither the capacity model of §6 nor the traffic model reads it: there is no sharing of prefix blocks between the branches of a beam and no copy traffic at a divergence. A beam of width W is represented as W independent sequences in the batch. That overstates memory, because the blocks of the common prefix are counted W times instead of once, and it leaves out the copy below.

Size of the omitted term. When a sequence branches into W beams, all beams share the common prefix, and each branch eventually writes into a block of its own, triggering at most W−1 block copies per divergence point. PagedAttention [VLLM] performs CoW at block granularity — only the one block being written to at the divergence point is copied, not the shared prefix history — so the extra traffic per divergence is bounded by

TCoW​≤(W−1)⋅Mblock​

with Mblock​ the per-device block size of §2. This is the size of one block per extra beam; the history read TKV,token​ is larger by the factor S/BLKKV​ (e.g., 256× for S=4096, BLKKV​=16). The copy traffic is therefore negligible against the baseline read, and the part of the omission that matters for sizing is the memory over-count of the shared prefix, which makes the capacity figures of §6 conservative for beam search.

4.3 Preemption and Recompute

When the block pool is exhausted (e.g., under bursty load or a request with unexpectedly long context), PagedAttention can preempt a running sequence by swapping its KV blocks to CPU DRAM or by discarding them entirely and recomputing on re-schedule [VLLM]. Both strategies introduce substantial overhead:

  • Swap: PCIe transfer at ~32–64 GB/s (vs. HBM at ~3 TB/s on H100), typically 50× slower. The traffic is the sequence’s per-device cache MKV,token​ in each direction.
  • Recompute: equivalent to re-running the prefill phase for the preempted sequence, contributing O(S2) FLOPs.

These overheads are workload-dependent, and the model of this document does not include them: it describes a block pool in steady state, without preemption, and no correction term stands in for them (framework.md §4.4). Their building blocks are priced elsewhere in this book: disaggregation.md gives the time to move a cache between GPU memory and host memory over a given path, and the bandwidth above which fetching a stored cache beats recomputing it. The design implication is that φ and MHBM,KV,avail​ should be sized conservatively to keep the block pool occupancy below ~85–90% in steady state, avoiding preemption entirely under expected workloads.

5. Interaction with TP and SP Sharding

Tensor Parallelism (TP)

Under TP-attention each TP rank holds Hkv​/TP of the head-channel dimension (for MLA, whose latent has no head structure, each rank holds the whole latent). Block allocation is TP-local: each rank independently manages its own shard of each block’s KV values. There is no cross-TP coordination required for paging; the block table on each TP rank contains physical addresses for that rank’s local KV shard.

Block size BLKKV​ is defined in terms of token positions (not channel elements), so it is invariant to TP degree. The fragmentation factor φ is likewise independent of TP.

Mode note (DP-attention). Under DP-attention mode (decode.md §1.4) the head-sharded KV layout above is replaced by a sequence-sharded layout: each TP rank holds full-head KV for 1/TP of the group’s sequences instead of 1/TP heads of all of them. For a GQA / MQA cache the per-device KV bytes and traffic are the same under either mode, which is why one divisor Dkv​ covers both (decode.md §1.4). The PagedAttention block accounting in this section applies to either layout — what changes is which sequences (vs which head-channels) live on a given device.

Sequence Parallelism (SP)

Each SP rank holds S/SP contiguous token positions from the KV sequence. Block allocation is per-SP-rank: each rank manages an independent block pool covering its S/SP token positions, with its own block table.

Alignment constraint: to avoid cross-shard block waste, BLKKV​ should divide S/SP evenly:

BLKKV​∣SPS​

If this condition is not met, each SP rank independently incurs last-block fragmentation on the boundary of its S/SP window, effectively multiplying the fragmentation overhead by SP for misaligned configurations.

Recommended practice: choose BLKKV​ such that BLKKV​≤S/(2⋅SP) to keep the per-rank fragmentation factor within 2:

φavg,SP-rank​≈1+2⋅(S/SP)BLKKV​​=1+2SBLKKV​⋅SP​

For SP>1, the effective fragmentation is therefore amplified by a factor of SP relative to the single-device case with the same BLKKV​ and S.

Pipeline Parallelism (PP)

Each PP stage owns L/PP disjoint layers and manages KV blocks for those layers independently. There is no cross-stage KV sharing or block table coordination. Fragmentation and capacity constraints apply independently within each PP stage; all stages have equal block pool size (assuming uniform layer assignment).

6. Effective HBM Capacity Model

Available HBM for KV storage

After subtracting parameter memory and activation workspace, the HBM available for KV blocks is:

MHBM,KV,avail​=MHBM​−Mθ,device​−Mact,device​−Msys​

where Msys​ is a system-level overhead reserve (CUDA context, kernel workspace, OS pages; typically 1–2 GB per GPU). Mθ,device​ and Mact,device​ are defined in decode.md §1.4.

KV capacity after fragmentation

The block pool can store at most MHBM,KV,avail​/Mblock​ physical blocks, but due to internal fragmentation only a fraction 1/φavg​ of that capacity holds useful token data. The effective KV storage capacity (in token-bytes at the device level) is:

MKV,capacity​=φavg​MHBM,KV,avail​​

Maximum supportable context length

Two conventions apply to the formulas below. The element width b in every KV term is the width of a cache element, bkv​: a serving stack stores the cache in its own data type, which need not equal the weight precision, and bkv​ equals the weight width b unless a narrower cache type is enabled. And the capacity is per device: under the orthogonal TP×EP layout each of the EP device groups holds the KV cache of its own share of the batch, so a replica holds Dbatch​=EP times as many concurrent sequences as one device’s capacity allows (the batch divisor of §1).

Combining with the per-sequence, per-device KV memory formula from §1, the maximum context length Smax​ of a single sequence satisfying the HBM constraint is:

PPL​⋅Dkv​⋅SP2Smax​Hkv​b​≤MKV,capacity​

Solving for Smax​:

Smax​=2Hkv​b⋅(L/PP)MKV,capacity​⋅Dkv​⋅SP​=φavg​⋅2Hkv​b⋅(L/PP)(MHBM​−Mθ,device​−Mact,device​−Msys​)⋅Dkv​⋅SP​

The divisor is Dkv​, not TP: the two coincide under the orthogonal layout but not in general, and for an MLA model under TP-attention the divisor is 1 and the numerator of the cache term is the latent (scope note).

Substituting φavg​≈1+BLKKV​/(2S) and noting that this gives an implicit equation in Smax​, the leading-order closed-form solution (valid when BLKKV​≪S) is obtained by evaluating φavg​≈1 on the right-hand side for a first estimate S^, then correcting:

Smax​≈1+BLKKV​/(2S^)S^​≈S^(1−2S^BLKKV​​)=S^−2BLKKV​​

where S^ is the contiguous-allocation estimate from decode.md §6.1:

S^=2Hkv​b⋅(L/PP)(MHBM​−Mθ,device​−Mact,device​)⋅Dkv​⋅SP​

The paging correction reduces Smax​ by exactly BLKKV​/2 tokens — one half-block per sequence — which is negligible for large contexts. The fragmentation penalty matters most in the regime S≲BLKKV​, where it can reduce usable capacity substantially.

Maximum concurrent sequences

Every sequence a device holds brings its cache and its activation working set. Let mseq​=φavg​⋅S⋅Mblock​/BLKKV​ be the paged cache of one sequence on one device, its S tokens times the average fragmentation factor of §3.1, and mact​ the activation working set one sequence adds (decode.md §1.4, per unit of batch). The room for sequences is what is left after the weights and the system reserve, so a replica holds at most

Nmax​=Dbatch​⋅⌊mseq​+mact​MHBM​−Mθ,device​−Msys​−(Nfly​/Dbatch​)⋅mseq​​⌋

concurrent sequences, where Dbatch​ is the batch divisor of §1. The activation term belongs in the denominator: charging activations once, at a fixed batch, would admit sequences whose working set was never counted. Nfly​ is the mean number of caches in flight to the replica during a disaggregated handoff (disaggregation.md §3); each already occupies the room of one sequence’s cache, but not its activations, and they are spread over the device groups like the batch. With Nfly​=0 and mact​≪mseq​ this is MHBM,KV,avail​/mseq​ per device. The token count in mseq​ is S itself and not the whole-block count Nblocks​(S)⋅BLKKV​: φavg​ already carries the partly filled last block, so rounding up as well would count it twice. With this definition the replica holds about Smax​/S sequences per device, consistent with the context limit above.

Summary: fragmentation-corrected HBM constraint

The HBM feasibility condition from decode.md §6.1 is refined by replacing the nominal KV capacity with the fragmentation-penalized version:

PPL​[Dattn​2H2+2HHkv​​+Dexp​3HINexp​​+φavg​⋅Bg​⋅Dkv​⋅SP2SHkv​​]b+Bg​(4H+2Hkv​)b+Demb​VH​b≤MHBM​−Msys​

The KV term carries the group batch Bg​=max(1,B/Dbatch​) of §1: every sequence the device holds brings its own cache, as it brings its own activation workspace in the next term. Dattn​, Dexp​ and Demb​ are the weight divisors of decode.md §1.4; under the orthogonal layout with TP-attention they are TP, TP⋅EP and TP. For φavg​=1 (contiguous allocation) and Msys​=0, this reduces exactly to the expression in §6.1 of decode.md.

Framework Overhead Model: Per-Phase Latency Constants

Author: Yue Lu
Date: April 2026

The hardware roofline model in decode.md establishes a lower bound on per-token decode latency, governed by compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. Real serving systems, however, introduce additional latency above this bound that lives entirely on the host CPU and serving-software path: tokenization at request entry, request scheduling and batch assembly, token sampling, and response streaming. These are empirical constants that require profiling on the target system — they cannot be derived from hardware specifications alone. This document catalogs the CPU / software-stack overhead terms, explains where each comes from, defines the per-request framework overhead tframework​ and shows how it enters time to first token (TTFT) and the latency of a whole request (§3), and lists the constants that describe each serving stack in the decode step itself, with the status of every value (§4). The kernel-launch and host-work terms that those constants feed are derived in decode.md §7; this document does not repeat the derivation. Hardware-level overheads tied to the network fabric (the transfer of a key-value (KV) cache between a prefill pool and a decode pool) are covered in disaggregation.md; memory-traffic calibration constants live in decode.md §6.2.

Two derivations cited below are companion documents that are not chapters of this book: the prefill and TTFT derivation, and the end-to-end metrics derivation. They are cited as plain text.

Table of Contents

  • 1. Overhead Classification
  • 2. CPU / Software-Stack Overhead Terms

    • 2.2 Request Scheduling and Batch Assembly
    • 2.3 Response Streaming and Detokenization
  • 3. Total Framework Overhead Per Request
  • 4. Per-Stack Constants of the Decode Step
    • 4.1 The Five Constants
    • 4.2 Values per Serving Stack
    • 4.3 Calibration Is per Setup
    • 4.4 What the Fitted Constants Absorb
  • 5. Symbol Summary

1. Overhead Classification

The table below catalogs the CPU / software-stack overhead terms, organized by the serving phase in which each occurs, the symbol used throughout this suite, and representative ranges from published sources and hardware measurements. All terms are empirical — they depend on the serving framework, OS, and CPU/tokenizer library path, and must be profiled on the target deployment.

OverheadPhaseChargedSymbolTypical Range
TokenizationPrefill entryonce per request, inside TTFTttok​~0.1–2 ms
Request scheduling / batch assemblyAdmissiononce per request, inside TTFTtsched​~10–200 µs
Response streaming / detokenizationDecodeonce per output tokentdetok​~1–10 µs/token

Out of scope for §1–§3. Host work that recurs on every decode step is not in this table: the kernel-launch dispatch budget tstage,kernel​ and the per-step host work tstep,seq​ (per-sequence bookkeeping plus a per-step floor) are composed inside the decode step time tstep,user​ in decode.md §7.1 and §7.3. §4 below lists their constants per serving stack. The language-model (LM) head H→V projection plus the sampling kernel that follows it (softmax, optional top-k / top-p, multinomial draw) are GPU-side per-step work and are modeled inside the per-step hardware roofline as the once-per-token tLM,hw​ term after the last pipeline-parallel (PP) stage (decode.md §2.1 / §3.5 / §6.2 / §7.2). The transfer of a KV cache from a prefill pool to a decode pool (an α–β network-fabric term) is derived in disaggregation.md.

2. CPU / Software-Stack Overhead Terms

Each subsection below describes what the term measures, why it exists at the systems level, how to calibrate it on a target deployment, and typical values from published sources where available.

2.1 Tokenization Latency

What it measures. ttok​ is the wall-clock time from receiving a raw text request to the point where token IDs are ready and the first CUDA kernel for the prefill pass is launched. It includes byte-pair encoding (BPE) or SentencePiece lookup, Unicode normalization, and any pre-processing applied by the serving framework.

Why it exists. Tokenization runs on CPU in most serving stacks (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, TGI). While GPU-side tokenization libraries exist, they are not universally deployed. The CPU→GPU handoff itself adds a small scheduling gap.

Scaling behavior. ttok​ scales weakly with input length: roughly O(Sinput​) character-level operations, but constant factors are small (BPE lookup is table-driven). For Sinput​≤4096 tokens the cost is typically 0.1–2 ms and is often pipelined with the previous request’s decode tail.

Calibration. Measure the latency from HTTP request receipt to the timestamp of the first cudaLaunchKernel call in a profiler trace (e.g., Nsight Systems). Vary Sinput​ to isolate the length-dependent component.

Typical values. 0.1–0.5 ms for short prompts (Sinput​≤512); up to 2 ms for very long prompts (Sinput​≈8192) on a single CPU thread. Parallelizing tokenization across CPU threads or pipelining it with KV allocation reduces the effective contribution to near zero for batch serving.

2.2 Request Scheduling and Batch Assembly

What it measures. tsched​ is the time the serving scheduler spends admitting one request: taking it from the queue, checking that its KV cache fits, allocating its KV pages, and preparing its batch metadata (token IDs, position IDs, block table) so that its prefill pass can launch. It is paid once per request, on the way in, and is part of TTFT (§3).

Why it exists. Before a request’s first kernel can launch, the scheduler must:

  1. Take the request from the priority queue of waiting requests.
  2. Estimate whether its KV cache pages fit in available HBM.
  3. Run the PagedAttention block allocator [VLLM] to assign physical KV blocks.
  4. Optionally, plan chunked-prefill piggybacking [SARATHI] for the request.
  5. Construct the attention metadata (block tables, sequence lengths) needed by the kernel.

All of this runs on CPU and must complete before the GPU kernel can launch.

What it is not. Continuous batching also makes the scheduler run between every two decode steps: it re-evaluates the active set, retires finished sequences and refreshes block tables. That recurring work is not tsched​. It is the per-step host work tstep,seq​(B)=corch​+cseq​⋅B of decode.md §7.3, which is charged on every decode step inside tstep,user​ and whose constants are listed per stack in §4. Keeping the two apart avoids charging the same work twice: tsched​ is the one-off admission of a request, tstep,seq​ is what the request costs the host on each step while it is active.

Calibration. Instrument the admission path with timestamps from request dequeue to the launch of its first kernel. Vary the number of concurrently active requests and the scheduler policy (first-come-first-served, preemptive, chunked prefill) to characterize the dependence on load.

Typical values. 10–50 µs under light load with simple first-come-first-served admission; 50–200 µs under heavy load (B≥64 active sequences) with full PagedAttention block allocation and chunked-prefill planning.

2.3 Response Streaming and Detokenization

What it measures. tdetok​ is the per-token cost of converting the sampled token ID back to a UTF-8 string fragment and transmitting it to the client (via HTTP chunked transfer or server-sent events).

Why it exists. Detokenization is the inverse of tokenization: a table lookup from token ID to byte sequence. It runs on CPU and is followed by a streaming write to the network socket. For most vocabulary sizes, the lookup itself is negligible; the dominant cost is the system call for the socket write plus any interpreter overhead in the serving framework.

Scaling behavior. tdetok​ applies once per generated token and is effectively constant in token output length (it does not grow with Tout​, only accumulates). The cumulative detokenization cost is Tout​×tdetok​, which is small relative to the total decode time for any non-trivially sized model.

Calibration. Measure round-trip latency from GPU token ID to client receipt at the application layer, minus network round-trip time (RTT). The residual is approximately tdetok​ (the sampling kernel after the LM head is folded into tLM,hw​ on the GPU side, not into this term).

Typical values. ~1–10 µs per token for the detokenization lookup itself. Socket write latency varies with network configuration and is separate from this constant.

3. Total Framework Overhead Per Request

Combining the CPU / software-stack overhead terms of §2, the framework’s share of a complete request — a prefill pass followed by decode steps, Tout​ output tokens in all — is:

tframework​=ttok​+tsched​+Tout​⋅tdetok​

The first two terms are paid once per request, the third once per output token. Kernel-launch dispatch and per-step host work are not in this sum — they are inside tstep,user​ (decode.md §7.1, §7.3). The LM head matrix multiply and the sampling kernel are likewise GPU-side and absorbed into tLM,hw​ inside tstep,user​ (decode.md §7.2).

Where the two per-request terms sit. Tokenization and scheduling happen before the prefill pass, so they are part of TTFT:

TTFT=tsched​+ttok​+tprefill​+tafter​

Here tprefill​ is the hardware prefill time (derived in the companion prefill document), which ends with the LM head on the last prompt position and therefore already yields the first token. When a prefill replica runs several prompts in one pass, every one of them waits for the whole pass, so tprefill​ is the time of the batched pass. tafter​ is whatever stands between the end of prefill and the emission of that token, and depends on who emits it:

Deploymenttafter​
Prefill and decode on the same replicathe repack of the cache into the decode layout, thandoff​; zero when the two phases use the same partition
Separate pools, the decode worker emits the first tokenthandoff​+tstep,user​: the decode worker waits for the cache, re-runs the last prompt position as one decode step, and emits the token
Separate pools, the prefill worker emits the first tokenzero; the transfer delays the second token instead

thandoff​ and the two-pool cases are derived in disaggregation.md.

Whole-request latency. The first token is the product of the prefill pass, so the remaining Tout​−1 tokens each take one decode step, and every token is streamed once:

ttotal​=TTFT+(Tout​−1)⋅tstep,user​+Tout​⋅tdetok​

In the third deployment of the table the handoff, which is not on the TTFT path, is added once (it lengthens the gap between the first and the second token). Because ttok​ and tsched​ are already inside TTFT, tframework​ must not be added on top of this expression: doing so would count tokenization and scheduling twice. Written with the framework’s share separated out, the same total is

ttotal​=(tprefill​+tafter​)+(Tout​−1)⋅tstep,user​+tframework​

The time per output token reported by the model is tstep,user​ alone; the streaming cost tdetok​ is reported beside it as a separate per-token figure and is not folded into it.

Order-of-magnitude comparison. For a representative decode-heavy workload (Tout​=512, greedy sampling, prefill and decode on the same replica):

TermPer-stepCumulative (Tout​=512)
tstep,user​ (hardware plus the kernel-launch budget and per-step host work of decode.md §7, and tLM,hw​)~2–20 ms1–10 s
tdetok​~5 µs~2.5 ms
ttok​ (once, inside TTFT)—~0.5 ms
tsched​ (once, inside TTFT)—~0.1 ms

The three terms of tframework​ are typically well under 1% of total request latency for well-optimized serving stacks on large models. The software stack’s larger contribution is inside the decode step, through the constants of §4.

4. Per-Stack Constants of the Decode Step

decode.md §7 turns the hardware stage time into the user-observed step time with two host-side terms: the kernel-launch dispatch budget of a stage, tstage,kernel​, and the per-step host work, tstep,seq​. Both are built from a handful of constants that describe the serving stack — the software that runs the model — and not the model, the hardware or the workload. This section lists them and gives the value used for each stack.

4.1 The Five Constants

ConstantMeaningEnters
τlaunch​Effective time to launch one GPU kernel (launch time)tstage,kernel​=τlaunch​× (kernels launched per stage pass), decode.md §7.1
ρkernel​Launch overlap: fraction of the stage’s hardware time behind which kernel dispatch hides, in [0,1]tstage,hw​+max(0,tstage,kernel​−ρkernel​⋅tstage,hw​), decode.md §7.2
cseq​Host work per active sequence per steptstep,seq​(B)=corch​+cseq​⋅B, decode.md §7.3
corch​Host work per step that does not depend on batchsame
ρseq​Host-work overlap: fraction of the per-step hardware window behind which host work hides, in [0,1]tstep,base​+max(0,tstep,seq​−ρseq​⋅tstep,base​), decode.md §7.3

An overlap of 1 means the host runs ahead of the GPU and its work costs nothing until it exceeds the hardware time it hides behind; an overlap of 0 means the two add. The kernel count that multiplies τlaunch​ uses the same three fan-out numbers for every stack: kcompute​=10 compute kernels per layer, kcollective​=2 kernels per collective call, and kpp_hop​=2 kernels per inter-stage hop. Because the count is the same flat figure everywhere, τlaunch​ is an effective launch time: it absorbs kernels that a captured graph does not cover and layers that launch more kernels than the flat count assumes (Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers in particular).

4.2 Values per Serving Stack

Serving stackτlaunch​ρkernel​cseq​corch​ρseq​Status
Neutral roofline (no stack chosen)1.5 µs1001A definition, not a stack: the launch budget acts only as a floor and no host work is charged.
TensorRT-LLM (compiled runtime, graph replay)1.5 µs175 µs01Starting point. The launch time is the usual figure for graph replay; cseq​ is the middle of the reported 50–100 µs range.
NVIDIA Dynamo wrapping TensorRT-LLM4 µs15 µs01Calibrated against measurement: the launch time on two models on one rack-scale system, and cseq​ at the level the per-setup fits return (3.0–5.5 µs).
NVIDIA Dynamo wrapping SGLang12 µs15 µs01The launch time is fitted on one measured setup; cseq​ and the overlaps are carried over from the row above and not fitted.
NVIDIA Dynamo wrapping vLLM8 µs15 µs01Unmeasured starting point: the launch time is a hypothesis placed between the two rows above, the rest is carried over.
vLLM10 µs0.340 µs00Unmeasured starting point: values chosen inside the ranges reported for interpreter-driven stacks.
SGLang10 µs0.340 µs00Unmeasured starting point, same reasoning as vLLM.

Reading the table:

  • Launch time. 1.5 µs is what graph replay costs when every kernel is inside the captured graph. The orchestrated compiled runtime sits at 4 µs, between that and the measured eager-mode floor of about 4.5–4.7 µs per launch [TAXBREAK], because expert routing and the per-step scheduler path stay outside the graph and MoE layers launch several times more kernels than the flat count. The interpreter-based runtimes keep 8–12 µs even under an orchestrator: the orchestrator absorbs per-sequence host work but does not remove the interpreter from the dispatch of kernels that fall outside the graph.
  • Launch overlap. 1 for the graph-replayed stacks, 0.3 for the two interpreter-driven ones, whose interpreter stalls prevent the host from running ahead. No stack description uses 0.
  • Host work per sequence. One value, 5 µs, for the three orchestrated stacks; 40 µs for the interpreter-driven stacks; 75 µs for the raw compiled runtime, which runs its per-sequence loop on the host between forward passes without an orchestrator to absorb it.
  • Host work per step. Zero in every stack description. It is non-zero only where it has been fitted to a measured setup (§4.3).
  • Host-work overlap. 1 for the graph-replayed stacks, 0 for the interpreter-driven ones.

Only two rows rest on measurement, and only for the constants named in their status. Every other value is a starting point to be replaced when the setup at hand is measured.

4.3 Calibration Is per Setup

A setup is one model on one system under one serving stack. The table of §4.2 is what the model uses for a stack before any measurement of the setup exists. When measured points of a setup are available, a few constants are fitted to them, and those fitted values replace the table’s values for that setup only.

What is shared and what is fitted:

  • Shared by the setups of a stack: the launch time τlaunch​, and the rule for whether host work hides behind the GPU step (ρseq​).
  • Fitted per setup, at most four constants: a multiplier on the sustained memory-bandwidth factor ηβ​ of decode.md §6.2; the per-sequence host work cseq​; the per-step floor corch​; and the launch overlap ρkernel​.

The fitted values show how far a setup can sit from its stack’s row. For the orchestrated compiled runtime on a rack-scale system, two setups (a 120-billion-parameter MoE model and a 671-billion-parameter MoE model with latent attention) return cseq​ of 5.5 and 4.8 µs, corch​ of zero and 0.62 ms, and ρkernel​ of 0.55 and 0.35, against the row’s 5 µs, zero and 1. For the raw compiled runtime on single-node systems, three setups return cseq​ of 49–85 µs and corch​ of 1.25–4.15 ms, against the row’s 75 µs and zero. In all of these fits the host work adds to the GPU step (ρseq​=0) rather than hiding behind it, although the stack rows carry ρseq​=1: on the measured setups the graph-replay assumption that the host runs ahead of the GPU is the optimistic end.

Three rules follow.

  1. Treat the fitted constants as residuals, not as measured properties of the software. They close the gap between a first-principles hardware model and a measurement, and they take up whatever the hardware model leaves out (§4.4).
  2. Do not carry a fit from one model to another. Constants fitted on one model and applied to a different model on the same hardware and stack leave errors several times larger than the fitted error. Report the error on points that were held out of the fit beside the fitted error.
  3. A stack row is a prior. For a setup that has not been measured, the row gives the right order of magnitude for a compiled, an orchestrated or an interpreter-driven stack, and no more.

4.4 What the Fitted Constants Absorb

The hardware model drops or omits a few effects, and none of them has a correction term of its own:

  • Residual activation traffic (decode.md §2.2): the hidden-state and feed-forward-network (FFN) buffer reads and writes that remain once the attention score matrix is kept out of device memory. On a measured setup it is absorbed by the fitted memory-bandwidth multiplier.
  • Normalization and elementwise compute (decode.md §3.4): absorbed by the sustained compute rate of the device and, at small batch, by the host constants.
  • Preemption, swap and recompute of a running sequence’s cache (kv.md §4.3): not modelled. A deployment that preempts is outside the steady state the step-time model describes; the cost of moving a cache to host memory and back, and of recomputing it instead, is priced in disaggregation.md.

The first two are the reason the fitted constants are residuals. The third is a limit of scope, not something a constant can absorb.

Service Level Objectives and the Partition Feasibility Boundary

Deriving B and (PP,TP,EP,SP) Bounds from TTFT and TPOT SLOs

1. SLOs as Operational Constraints

A service-level objective (SLO) is an operator-set upper bound on a user-observed latency metric, paired with a compliance percentile (typically the 90th, 95th, or 99th). The serving system is expected to keep the metric below the bound for at least the specified percentile of requests. SLOs are the primary mechanism by which production deployments translate user-experience requirements (“first token within 500 ms,” “5 tokens/s streaming or better”) into operational constraints on the serving stack — and through the roofline composed in decode.md §6.2 and in the companion prefill derivation (§3.4 there; not a chapter of this book), into hard bounds on the partition shape (PP,TP,EP,SP) and the operating batch size B.

This document derives those bounds. Section 2 inverts the decode roofline to produce Bmax​ as a function of TPOTSLO​ at a given partition shape; Section 3 reads the prefill roofline against TTFTSLO​ at a given input-prompt length — a floor on how wide the shape must be, and only a weak bound on pipeline depth; Section 4 intersects the two bounds (plus a dynamic batch window) to define the feasibility region; Section 5 frames partition choice as goodput maximization over that region. Section 6 maps common workload classes onto representative SLO targets.

The goodput definition itself is established in the companion end-to-end metrics derivation (§1.5 there; not a chapter of this book) and is restated in §1.3 below; this document treats that definition as the canonical statement and builds the partition-feasibility derivation on top of it.

1.1 The Two Canonical SLOs

Production LLM inference frameworks ([VLLM], [DYNAMO], [TENSORRT-LLM]) almost universally expose two latency-side SLOs:

  • TTFTSLO​ — time-to-first-token (TTFT) bound. Operator-set upper bound on the time from request admission to the first output token reaching the user. Typical targets: 200 ms (interactive chat), 500 ms (multi-turn assistant), 2 s (batch document tasks).
  • TPOTSLO​ — time-per-output-token (TPOT) bound. Operator-set upper bound on the inter-token latency during the streaming decode phase. Typical targets: 50 ms (15 tokens/s, “comfortable reading speed”), 100 ms (10 tokens/s, “live streaming”), 200 ms (5 tokens/s, “minimum viable streaming”). Below 5 tokens/s the user perceives the response as stalled rather than streaming.

A request meets the joint SLO if both its TTFT and its full-response mean TPOT fall below the respective bounds. Both are user-observable: TTFT determines the “feels responsive?” judgment a user makes within the first second; TPOT determines whether the streaming output is comfortable to read or feels sluggish. The two metrics are produced by structurally different serving phases (compute-bound prefill versus memory-bound decode) and therefore have different sensitivities to the partition shape — a misalignment that drives much of the production architecture choice analyzed in §3.3.

Throughput-side SLOs (requests/second per replica, tokens/second per cluster) exist but are typically derived quantities. For a fixed latency-SLO pair, the maximum sustainable arrival rate λ is uniquely determined — that quantity is the goodput defined in §1.3, and it serves as the optimization target rather than an independent constraint.

Other latency-side SLOs occasionally surface in production (end-to-end response-completion deadline, cancellation-tolerant best-effort tail) but reduce in our framework to one of the two canonical SLOs above plus a fixed output-length distribution; we focus on the canonical pair throughout.

1.2 The Compliance Percentile p

The SLO is met “at percentile p” when at least p% of requests fall below the bound. The choice of p has non-trivial consequences for partition choice because the per-request distribution of TTFT and TPOT is non-Gaussian and right-skewed under realistic traffic patterns:

  • Mean-driven SLOs (p=50, equivalently a target on E[TPOT]). Easy to satisfy and easy to model; the steady-state roofline composition in decode.md §6.2 directly produces a mean-TPOT estimate. Mean-driven SLOs are typical in offline batch evaluation, internal service-level agreements without strict user-experience claims, and synthetic benchmarks (most published throughput–latency curves implicitly use p≤50).
  • Tail-driven SLOs (p∈{90,95,99}). The standard for user-facing production deployments. Tail-driven SLOs penalize variance: a serving stack whose mean-TPOT is well within the bound but whose p99 spikes during batch surges, KV-cache eviction, or admission-control queuing fails the SLO and is operationally non-viable.

For analytical modeling we work with the mean throughout the derivations of §2 and §3, then add a tail-cushion margin in §4.3 to translate mean-driven feasibility into tail-driven feasibility. This factorization mirrors the [DISAGG-PREFILL] approach: derive the mean-TPOT and mean-TTFT bounds from a roofline, then verify the percentile bound through simulation or empirical workload replay.

The cushion is non-trivial because tail amplification is partition-shape-dependent. Deeper PP narrows the dynamic-stability margin (§4.2), so tail-TPOT under bursty traffic can be much larger than mean-TPOT for the same shape — even when mean-TPOT looks comfortable. This is one of the structural reasons production frameworks default to shallower PP than the steady-state roofline would prefer.

1.3 Goodput as the Optimization Target

A serving cluster does not operate at a single (B,λ) point: it operates over a range of arrival rates, with B varying iteration-to-iteration as the continuous-batching scheduler admits and retires requests (companion end-to-end derivation, §3.2). The natural optimization target is therefore not “maximize throughput” but maximize the arrival rate λ that the cluster can sustain while keeping both SLOs satisfied at percentile p. This quantity is the goodput, defined in the companion end-to-end derivation (§1.5) as:

Goodput=maxλs.t.Pp​[TTFT(λ)]≤TTFTSLO​andPp​[TPOT(λ)]≤TPOTSLO​

Goodput differs from raw throughput in three operationally important ways. (1) Throughput counts every token emitted; goodput counts only tokens emitted by requests that met the SLO. A cluster running at 100% utilization but failing the p99 SLO has high throughput and zero goodput from a contractual standpoint. (2) Goodput is the binding metric for production capacity planning: the number of replicas required to serve a given request rate is ⌈λoffered​/Goodput⌉, not ⌈λoffered​/Throughputmax​⌉. (3) Goodput is the right comparison axis when evaluating partition shapes or hardware platforms — a hardware configuration that achieves higher peak throughput but lower goodput is a worse production deployment, full stop.

The goodput framework was formalized by [ALPASERVE] (statistical multiplexing across SLO-bound replicas) and adopted as the optimization target by [DISAGG-PREFILL] (DistServe), [SPLITWISE] (phase-split SLO co-design), and [MOONCAKE]. The conceptual move — from throughput to goodput as the figure of merit — is now standard in serving-systems research and informs the production defaults of [VLLM], [TENSORRT-LLM], and [DYNAMO]. We adopt it as the framework’s optimization target; the rest of this document derives the constraints that define the feasibility region over which goodput is maximized.

2. The TPOT-SLO to Maximum-Batch Mapping

The TPOT-SLO bounds the per-step decode latency tstep,user​(B), which in turn bounds the operating batch size B by a maximum Bmax​. The bound is non-trivial because tstep,user​(B) is non-monotone-flat in B — it sits at a memory-bound floor up to the crossover batch B⋆ from decode.md §4, then grows linearly past it. The TPOT-SLO either falls in the flat region (in which case the bound is loose and not binding), the linear region (in which case the bound is tight and gives a closed-form Bmax​), or below the floor (in which case no B satisfies the SLO at the current partition shape, and the partition is infeasible).

Speculative-decoding extension. When the deployment runs with speculative decoding enabled (Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) / EAGLE / Medusa, decode.md §8), the user-observed TPOT is TPOTspec​(B)=tstep,userverify​(B)/Ntok/step​ rather than tstep,user​(B). The SLO then bounds TPOTspec​, and both the verify-step floor and the verify-step crossover Bspec⋆​ from decode.md §8.4 substitute for their vanilla counterparts in the analysis below. In the memory-bound regime — the dominant operating regime for MoE / MLA decode at production batch sizes — the substitution is a clean 1/Ntok/step​ scaling on TPOT and the §2.2 Zone 1 / Zone 2 / Zone 3 partition-feasibility argument carries through unchanged.

2.1 Inverting the Decode Roofline

The full decode-step time from decode.md §7.3 is:

tstep,user​(B)=PP⋅[tstage,hw​(Bmb​)+max(0,tstage,kernel​−ρkernel​tstage,hw​(Bmb​))]+tLM,hw​(Bmb​)

where Bmb​=max(1,B/PP) is the microbatch one pipeline stage processes per pass (a token crosses all PP stages, decode.md §7.2), tstage,hw​ is the overlap-aware per-stage hardware roofline (decode.md §6.2), tstage,kernel​ is the per-stage CPU/host kernel-launch dispatch budget (decode.md §7.1), ρkernel​ is the dispatch-overlap factor, and tLM,hw​(B) is the once-per-step LM head H→V projection on stage PP−1.

For batch sizes B≥PP (the pipeline-full regime, see §4.2 for why this is the operational target) every stage is busy and Bmb​=B/PP. The hardware stage time itself is a max-of-rooflines:

tstage,hw​(B)=tstage,local​(B)+max(0,tstage,comm​(B)−ρcomm​tstage,local​(B))

with the local term given by the compute/memory roofline:

tstage,local​(B)=max(RGPU​B⋅Ftoken,device​​,BWmem​Tθ,device​+B⋅TKV,device​​)

The dependence on B is qualitatively simple: tstage,local​ is approximately constant in B for B≪B⋆ (weight-stream-bound, the Tθ,device​/BWmem​ term dominates) and grows linearly in B for B≫B⋆ (compute-bound, the B⋅Ftoken,device​/RGPU​ term dominates). Setting tstep,user​(B)=TPOTSLO​ and solving for B gives Bmax​. We carry the algebra zone-by-zone in §2.2 because the closed-form expression and the operational interpretation differ across zones.

2.2 Three Roofline Zones Reread as SLO Regimes

The decode roofline has three zones in B (developed in full in the companion end-to-end derivation, §6.2); the TPOT-SLO bound looks structurally different in each.

Zone 1 — Memory-bound floor (B≪B⋆)

The step time sits at the weight-streaming floor:

tstep,user​(B)≈BWmem​Tθ,device​​(B≪B⋆)

If TPOTSLO​>Tθ,device​/BWmem​, the SLO is satisfied at every B in the memory-bound regime; Bmax​ is then determined by the Zone-3 ceiling below, not by Zone 1. If TPOTSLO​<Tθ,device​/BWmem​, no B satisfies the SLO at this partition shape — the weight read on a token’s path is too long, and a wider sharding that divides it in parallel (larger TP or EP) is required. Deeper PP does not help here: it shrinks Tθ,device​ per stage by 1/PP, but the token crosses PP stages, so the product PP⋅Tθ,device​/BWmem​ is unchanged. This is the cleanest, most operationally consequential SLO bound: it tells the partition optimizer that a candidate shape is infeasible before any batch-size sweep begins.

Zone 2 — Crossover knee (B≈B⋆)

The system operates at the ridge point; both rooflines contribute comparably to tstep,user​. For SLO purposes, Zone 2 is the natural operating point: throughput-per-GPU has saturated near the compute ceiling, and per-user latency has not yet started degrading. A well-tuned production deployment targets B≈B⋆ at peak load.

Zone 3 — Compute-bound ceiling (B≫B⋆)

The step time grows linearly with B:

tstep,user​(B)≈RGPU​B⋅Ftoken,device​​(B≫B⋆)

Setting equal to TPOTSLO​ and solving yields the SLO-bound batch size:

Bmax​≈Ftoken,device​RGPU​⋅TPOTSLO​​​(Zone 3)

This is the operationally tight bound for any deployment that has crossed B⋆. It is independent of Tθ,device​ — once compute-bound, the per-device weight footprint no longer affects per-step time — and depends only on the compute capacity per device RGPU​ (FLOPS), the per-token FLOPs Ftoken,device​ (model architecture and partition shape), and the SLO target itself.

Combined feasibility condition

A partition shape (PP,TP,EP,SP) at sequence length S is TPOT-feasible if and only if the Zone 1 floor is below the SLO:

BWmem​Tθ,device​(PP,TP,EP,SP)​≤TPOTSLO​

For partition shapes that pass this check, Bmax​ is given by the Zone-3 expression above, capped by the HBM capacity bound (decode.md §1.4) — at most B KV-caches must fit in HBM alongside the weights and activation buffers. The full feasibility condition for the partition-batch tuple is:

B≤min​TPOT-SLO boundFtoken,device​RGPU​⋅TPOTSLO​​​​,HBM boundTKV,device​⋅SHBMfree​​​​​subject toBWmem​Tθ,device​​≤TPOTSLO​

where HBMfree​ is the HBM remaining after weights and activations are accounted for. The TPOT-SLO bound is decode-roofline-derived; the HBM bound is capacity-derived. Whichever binds first sets the operating Bmax​.

2.3 Worked Example — GPT-1.8T MoE on NVL72

Concrete numbers make the bound tangible. Take the GPT-1.8T mixture-of-experts (MoE) model used elsewhere in the framework’s partition sweeps, served on a 72-GPU NVL72 rack at FP4 quantization (bytes per parameter b=0.5). Baseline parameters: L=120 layers, H=18432 hidden, nq​=128 query heads, nkv​=16 KV heads, dense FFN intermediate Idense​=H, MoE intermediate Imoe​=H/2, nexperts​=16, kactive​=2. NVL72 device specs: RGPU​=2.5PFLOPS at FP4, BWmem​=8TB/s.

Consider a candidate partition shape PP=8, TP=8, EP=1, SP=1 (NGPUs,per−replica​=64, DP=1). Per-device weight footprint at FP4 is approximately Tθ,device​≈14GB (full model 1.8 TB, sharded across 64 devices, with the MoE expert weights paged across the EP axis if EP>1). The Zone-1 floor is then:

tstep,userfloor​≈8TB/s14GB​=1.75ms

Three SLO scenarios:

TPOTSLO​Workload classFloor checkBmax​ from Zone-3 bound
100 mslive streaming, 10 tok/s1.75≤100 ✓≈Ftoken,device​2.5⋅1015⋅0.1​≈100–200
50 mscomfortable reading, 15 tok/s1.75≤50 ✓≈50–100
30 mstight conversational, 30 tok/s1.75≤30 ✓≈30–60

The exact Zone-3 numbers depend on Ftoken,device​ which scales as L⋅H2/NGPUs,per−replica​ for the dense and active-expert paths (decode.md §3); the order of magnitude is what matters here. At the conversational target (TPOTSLO​=30ms) and Bmax​≈50, the operating point is well inside the memory-bound regime (where B⋆ for this shape is typically 64–256 at decode, see decode.md §4 for the formula). The TPOT-SLO does not bind in Zone 3; the HBM-capacity bound binds instead, since 50 sequences with S=8192 KV cache exceed the per-device HBM headroom.

Two takeaways. (i) For tight-conversational SLOs on dense-attention workloads, the binding constraint is rarely the TPOT-SLO itself — it is the HBM-capacity bound or (equivalently) the memory-bound floor. The role of the TPOT-SLO is to eliminate partition shapes whose floor is too high, not to set a tight Bmax​. (ii) Pushing into Zone 3 to maximize per-GPU throughput requires either a very loose TPOT-SLO (batch / async workloads, see §6.3) or a partition shape whose Ftoken,device​ has been driven low enough by TP / EP sharding to keep B⋅F/R under the SLO. The latter is exactly the partition-vs-SLO co-design loop that §5 formalizes.

3. The TTFT-SLO and Partition Shape

The TTFT-SLO bounds the time from request admission to first output token, which composes the scheduling overhead, the prefill forward pass, and — under disaggregation — the inter-cluster KV transfer and the decode step that emits the token (framework.md §3 gives the composition). The component most sensitive to partition shape is the prefill forward pass. Pipeline depth enters it only through the inter-stage hops, so the bound it places on PP is weak; the binding constraint is on how much the prefill work is divided in parallel.

3.1 What Pipeline Depth Costs in TTFT

From the companion prefill derivation (§3.3 / §3.4 there), the prefill forward pass for a single request traverses all PP pipeline stages sequentially before the first token can be sampled. Unlike decode, prefill has no inflight microbatching across stages on a single unchunked request — the prompt is one indivisible work unit:

tprefill​=PP⋅[tprefill,local​(Sinput​)+max(0,tprefill,comm​−ρcomm​tprefill,local​)]+tLM,prefill,hw​

Each stage holds L/PP layers, so tprefill,local​ and the collective part of tprefill,comm​ are 1/PP of their single-stage values and the bracket times PP does not move. The only term that grows with depth is the inter-stage hop inside tprefill,comm​: one per stage. Writing tprefill(1)​ for the single-stage prefill time and tPPprefill​ for one hop:

tprefill​(PP)≈tprefill(1)​+(PP−1)⋅(1−ρcomm​)⋅tPPprefill​

Setting the single-request co-located TTFT, tsched​+tprefill​, equal to TTFTSLO​ and solving for PP:

PPmax​≈1+(1−ρcomm​)⋅tPPprefill​TTFTSLO​−tsched​−tprefill(1)​(Sinput​)​​

The hop carries Sinput​ tokens of activations, so on an intra-node fabric it is microseconds to a fraction of a millisecond and PPmax​ is large — depth is rarely what breaks a TTFT target. On a slow cross-node fabric with long prompts the hop can reach milliseconds and the bound tightens. The floor check is the stricter one: if tsched​+tprefill(1)​>TTFTSLO​, no pipeline depth helps, because depth does not shorten the prefill.

The partition consequence: TTFT is reduced by sharding that divides the prefill work in parallel — TP, and SP for the attention term — and is indifferent to PP apart from the hops. TPOT-SLO has the same structure (§2.2 Zone 1). The two SLOs therefore agree on the axis: both want width, not depth. PP remains what it is for decode — a way to fit a model or a batch in memory (the companion prefill derivation, §6, covers the same observation from the prefill side). An earlier version of this section derived a tight PPmax​ from a warmup term (PP−1)⋅tstage,max​ treated as independent of PP; that overlooked the 1/PP scaling of the stage time and overstated the TTFT cost of depth.

3.2 Chunked Prefill: Where Depth Does Help TTFT

[SARATHI] introduces chunked prefill: split the prefill of a single request into Nchunks​=⌈Sinput​/C⌉ smaller chunks of C tokens each, and interleave each chunk with a decode iteration. The motivation in [SARATHI] is to reduce head-of-line blocking — long prefill passes can stall the decode pipeline for tens to hundreds of milliseconds, inflating decode-phase TPOT for all in-flight requests.

Chunking also changes what pipeline depth does. A layer’s keys and values for chunk k are final once that layer has processed chunk k, so chunk k+1 can enter the first stage as soon as chunk k has left it: successive chunks of one prompt occupy successive stages. The first stage sees the chunks back to back, each at a single-stage cost, and the last chunk then crosses the remaining stages (companion prefill derivation, §5.2):

TTFTchunked​≈tsched​+k=1∑Nchunks​​tchunk(k)​+(PP−1)⋅tchunk(Nchunks​)​+tLM,prefill,hw​

with each tchunk(k)​ the time for chunk k on one stage, which holds L/PP layers. For uniform chunks the body is (Nchunks​+PP−1) stage-chunk times against Nchunks​⋅PP without overlap, so with many more chunks than stages the prefill approaches 1/PP of its single-stage time. This is the one place in the model where pipeline depth shortens a latency: the unchunked prompt is one indivisible unit and gets nothing from depth (§3.1); the chunked prompt is a stream of units and does.

Two things limit the gain in practice. Each chunk re-reads the weights of the stage it is on, so in the memory-bound regime (small C) the per-chunk cost does not shrink with C and many small chunks cost more than one large pass. And when chunks are interleaved with decode iterations, as [SARATHI] intends, they are not back to back: the gaps are set by the decode step, not by the stage time. Typical production tunings sit at C∈[512,2048], balancing head-of-line relief against per-chunk overhead.

3.3 Disaggregation When the Two Phases Want Different Shapes

The TTFT-SLO and the TPOT-SLO agree on the axis — both want width (§3.1) — but not on the shape. Prefill is compute-bound at typical Sinput​, runs best at a batch near one, and wants its width sized to the prompt’s compute. Decode is memory-bound, runs best at a large batch, and wants width (and sometimes depth) sized to the weight read and to the KV cache of many concurrent sequences. A co-located deployment must pick one shape for both, and its prefill passes interrupt its decode steps. Disaggregated prefill [DISAGG-PREFILL] runs the two phases on physically separate workers with independent partition shapes, connected by a KV-cache transfer.

[DISAGG-PREFILL] (DistServe), [SPLITWISE] (phase-split co-design), and [MOONCAKE] (KV-centric architecture) all motivate disaggregation through this asymmetry, and the production deployment in [DYNAMO] adopts it. The cost of disaggregation is the KV-cache transfer:

tKV-transfer​=max(0,αinter​+BWinter​MKV​​−ρKV​⋅tprefill​)

where MKV​=2L⋅Sinput​⋅Hkv​⋅bkv​ is the prompt’s KV cache and ρKV​ is the fraction of the transfer that overlaps the prefill pass under layer-wise streaming (disaggregation.md §3). Whether disaggregation improves TTFT depends on which worker emits the first token (framework.md §3):

co-locatedtprefill​(shapeco​)​​vs.disaggregated, decode worker emitstprefill​(shapeprefill​)+tKV-transfer​+tstep,user​​​vs.disaggregated, prefill worker emitstprefill​(shapeprefill​)​​

On the hardware terms alone, disaggregation helps TTFT only by as much as the dedicated prefill shape is faster than the shared one, and — when the decode worker emits — costs the visible transfer and one decode step. Layer-wise KV streaming ([MOONCAKE], [SPLITWISE]) drives the visible transfer toward zero when the link is fast relative to the prefill. What this comparison leaves out is the term that motivates the architecture in the first place: on a shared worker, a request’s prefill waits behind decode steps and other prefills, and every prefill pass stalls the tokens of the sequences already decoding. That interference is not in the roofline of either phase, so the comparison above understates the benefit.

disaggregation.md §5 prices that interference for a time-sliced shared worker. With d the fraction of the worker’s time spent in prefill, its mean time per output token is TPOT(B)/(1−d) and its worst gap between two tokens is one step plus one prefill pass (or one chunk). Two results from there bear on this section. First, with the same shape in both pools and a transfer that costs no device time, a shared pool and a balanced split have the same mean throughput per device, so the benefit of disaggregation is not in the mean. Second, a TPOTSLO​ caps the prefill duty of a shared worker at 1−TPOT(B)/TPOTSLO​ and therefore its request rate, while a decode pool only needs TPOT(B)≤TPOTSLO​; the gain appears as a larger request rate inside the SLO and grows as the SLO tightens.

The goodput improvement from disaggregation comes from a second source: independent scaling. A co-located cluster sized for the larger of the two SLO footprints (typically decode) underutilizes the over-provisioned dimension; a disaggregated cluster sizes prefill and decode independently and runs each at its own goodput optimum. [DISAGG-PREFILL] reports goodput improvements of 2–4× on workloads where prefill and decode preferences diverge (long prompts with short responses, or short prompts with long responses). The tradeoff is operational complexity: two clusters, two scheduling decisions, KV-transfer protocol, and request-routing logic.

For our framework’s purposes, the disaggregation analysis collapses into a simple decision rule. Compute the goodput-optimal partition under the two-pool assumption (separate prefill and decode shapes); compute it under the one-pool constraint (one shape for both); the larger of the two goodputs identifies whether disaggregation is beneficial at the offered workload mix. We return to this in §5.

4. The Joint Feasibility Region

The bounds from §2 (Bmax​ from TPOTSLO​) and §3 (the TTFT floor and the weak PPmax​ from TTFTSLO​) are independent constraints — both must hold for a deployment to meet the joint SLO. Together with HBM capacity, dynamic-stability, and tail-cushion margins, they define the feasibility region: the set of (PP,TP,EP,SP,B) tuples over which goodput maximization (§5) is performed.

4.1 Both SLOs Must Hold

The joint feasibility region is the intersection of the per-SLO regions:

FSLO​={(PP,TP,EP,SP,B)​TPOT floorPP⋅BWmem​Tθ,device​​≤TPOTSLO​​​∧TPOT boundB≤Bmax​​​∧TTFT boundtsched​+tprefill​≤TTFTSLO​​​∧capacityHBMused​(B)≤HBMcapacity​​​}

A partition shape that fails the TPOT floor is structurally infeasible: no batch size B rescues it. A partition shape that passes the TPOT floor but whose prefill does not fit the TTFT budget is prefill-infeasible: it can sustain decode but cannot deliver first tokens in time. Since prefill time is set by width and is nearly flat in PP (§3.1), the remedy is a wider shape or a separate prefill pool, not a shallower pipeline. A shape that satisfies both SLO bounds but exceeds HBM capacity at the SLO-bound B is capacity-infeasible.

The first prune (TPOT floor) is the cheapest to apply and eliminates the largest fraction of the partition space; we run it first in §5.2’s sweep recipe. Among shapes that pass the floor, the joint constraint B≤min(Bmax​,BHBM​) produces the tight per-shape operating bound. The TTFT bound depends on the shape and the prompt length but not on the decode batch, so it can be evaluated independently of B.

4.2 Static vs. Dynamic Feasibility — the Batch Window

The bounds in §2 and §3 are static — they assume a steady-state operating point. Production traffic is not steady-state: arrivals are bursty (Poisson at best, often heavier-tailed), individual requests complete asynchronously as their stop tokens fire, and sequence lengths vary by orders of magnitude across requests. The active-batch count B(t) at any instant is a stochastic process that fluctuates around its mean B, and the two directions of fluctuation cost different things.

Surges cost latency. A token crosses all PP stages in a microbatch of B(t)/PP sequences, so TPOT rises with the instantaneous batch (decode.md §7.2). For a tail-driven SLO at percentile p it is the upper tail of B(t) that must stay inside the latency bound:

TPOT(B+Δdyn​(p,σB​))≤TPOTSLO​⟺B≤BSLO​−Δdyn​(p,σB​)

where BSLO​ is the static TPOT bound on B from §2 and σB​ is the standard deviation of B(t) under the offered load. Concretely, Δdyn​≈zp​⋅σB​ where zp​ is the standard-normal p-quantile (1.28 for p90, 2.33 for p99). For Poisson arrivals at request rate λ with mean sojourn time τˉ, B=λτˉ and σB​=λτˉ​, giving Δdyn​≈zp​B​ — a square-root scaling. For p99 at B=100, the cushion is ≈23: the operating mean must sit 23 below the static bound.

Dips cost hardware, not latency. When B(t) falls below PP there are fewer microbatches than stages and PP−B(t) stages idle. The sequences that remain run at a microbatch of one and their tokens come no slower — a dip cannot violate a TPOT bound. What it lowers is the fraction of the pipeline doing useful work, min(1,B(t)/PP), and therefore goodput per device. Keeping every stage busy at confidence p requires

B≥PP+Δdyn​(p,σB​)

which is an efficiency condition: violating it wastes devices without breaking the SLO.

Together the two give the window in which a deployment is both SLO-feasible in the tail and fully used:

PP+Δdyn​≤B≤BSLO​−Δdyn​

Two operational implications. (i) Deeper PP narrows the window from below. A deployment sized for PP=60 needs B≥80 at p99 to keep its stages busy; one sized for PP=8 needs B≥12. The required arrival rate to sustain the larger B scales accordingly (Little’s Law; companion end-to-end derivation, §3.2), and when the window closes (PP+2Δdyn​>BSLO​) no operating point is both efficient and SLO-feasible at that depth: the deployment must run underfilled. (ii) The lower edge is one reason production prefers TP-first over PP-first, alongside the more basic one that pipeline depth does not shorten a token’s path at all: TP carries no minimum-batch requirement, since all of its ranks work on every token whatever the active-batch count. EP under the orthogonal layout has a milder version of the same edge — with fewer sequences than expert-parallel groups, some groups idle during attention.

The bound on Δdyn​ depends on the workload model (Poisson, Gamma-distributed sojourn, heavier-tailed bursts) and the scheduler’s admission-control policy; rigorous derivation is deferred to the simulation framework. For the analytical feasibility region we use the conservative rule 1.5⋅PP≤B≤BSLO​/1.5 at p99, which absorbs the zp​B​ cushion on both sides for realistic operating points.

4.3 Why p99 Narrows the Region

The mean-driven feasibility region of §4.1 ignores variance; the tail-driven version of §4.2 absorbs batch variance into the cushion. A third source of variance is sequence-length variance: requests with longer prompts inflate the prefill pass and longer decode tails inflate per-step compute. For a tail-driven TTFTSLO​ at p99, the binding scenario is the longest-prompt request — and the partition shape must satisfy the TTFT bound at Sinput,max​ (or the p99 of the prompt-length distribution), not at Sinput​​. Because prefill time grows at least linearly with prompt length, this typically tightens the TTFT floor — the width the shape needs — by the ratio of the p99 to the mean prompt length.

For TPOT, the analogous tail effect is sequence-length-induced KV-cache growth: a long-decode request accumulates KV traffic linearly in S, eventually pushing TKV,device​ above the threshold where B⋆ collapses (decode.md §4 no-crossover regime). The p99 TPOT for the long-tailed sequence-length distribution can be substantially higher than the mean — and the tail-feasibility bound on Bmax​ is correspondingly tighter than the mean bound from §2.2.

These tail effects are workload-distribution-dependent and not captured analytically in our roofline framework; they require empirical workload profiling or distribution-aware simulation. For partition-feasibility analysis we apply the cushion factors (typically the p99 prompt length in the TTFT bound and 0.7× on Bmax​ for p99 vs. mean) and verify the result against profiling data. The framework’s published partition sweeps use mean-driven bounds to keep the sweep computationally tractable; the tail cushions are applied at deployment time.

5. Goodput-Optimal Partition

The feasibility region of §4 defines what is allowed; the goodput function of §1.3 defines what is optimal. Goodput-optimal partition choice is the maximization of the goodput over the feasibility region — a constrained optimization problem with a tractable structure, which we develop as a sweep recipe.

5.1 Goodput as Objective, SLOs as Constraints

Restated formally:

(PP,TP,EP,SP)∈FSLO​max​Goodput(PP,TP,EP,SP)=TTFT+Nout​⋅TPOTBop​(PP,TP,EP,SP)​

via Little’s Law (companion end-to-end derivation, §3.2), where Bop​ is the SLO-feasible operating batch (the smaller of Bmax​ and the HBM bound), and TTFT, TPOT are the mean-driven values at Bop​. The goodput is dimensioned as requests/second/replica; multiplying by DP gives the cluster goodput.

The structure of the maximum. Because Bop​ enters the numerator and TPOT enters the denominator, and because both are functions of the partition shape with opposite-sign sensitivities, the goodput function has interior maxima — there is generally a “sweet spot” partition rather than a corner solution. The TPOT-SLO floor (§2.2) eliminates the corner of too little sharding (per-device weight footprint above the floor); the TTFT-SLO bound (§3.1) eliminates the corner of too much PP; the HBM bound eliminates the corner of too much B. Within those constraints, the goodput-optimal point typically sits at moderate sharding with B≈B⋆ — exactly the Zone-2 knee that the companion end-to-end derivation (§6.2) identifies as the natural production operating point.

5.2 Sweep Recipe

The feasibility region is discrete (factor combinations of PP, TP, EP, SP that divide the device count) and small (typically a few hundred candidate shapes for a 64–256 device cluster). Brute-force enumeration is computationally trivial. The sweep:

  1. Enumerate partition shapes. For each integer factorization N=PP⋅TP⋅EP⋅SP⋅DP of the device count, generate the candidate (PP,TP,EP,SP) tuple.

  2. Apply the TPOT floor. Compute Tθ,device​(PP,TP,EP,SP) from decode.md §1.4; reject shapes where PP⋅Tθ,device​/BWmem​>TPOTSLO​ (a token reads the weights of every stage it crosses).

  3. Apply the TTFT bound. Compute tprefill​(Sinput​) for the shape from the companion prefill derivation (§3); reject shapes where tsched​+tprefill​>TTFTSLO​.

  4. Solve for Bop​. For each surviving shape, compute Bmax​ from the Zone-3 expression in §2.2 and BHBM​ from the capacity bound; set Bop​=min(Bmax​,BHBM​). If Bop​<1 the shape is infeasible; reject.

  5. Apply the batch window. For surviving shapes, verify 1.5⋅PP≤Bop​≤Bmax​/1.5 (§4.2). The upper edge is an SLO condition (tail latency under batch surges); the lower edge is an efficiency condition (idle stages), so a shape that fails only the lower edge is wasteful, not infeasible.

  6. Compute goodput. Evaluate the goodput function from §5.1 at (PP,TP,EP,SP,Bop​). Rank surviving shapes by goodput.

  7. Co-located vs. disaggregated comparison. Repeat steps 1–6 under the disaggregated assumption with independent prefill and decode shapes; if the disaggregated maximum exceeds the co-located maximum by more than a workload-specific threshold (typically 10–20% to compensate for operational complexity), recommend disaggregation [DISAGG-PREFILL].

The framework’s notebooks/ partition sweeps implement steps 1, 2, 4, and 6 directly; the TTFT bound (step 3) and the dynamic-stability cushion (step 5) are applied as post-filters when SLO-aware analysis is required. The disaggregated comparison (step 7) is currently a manual analysis driven by workload-mix awareness; automating it would require an integrated prefill+decode optimizer, which is a natural extension of the analytical framework but beyond the current scope.

5.3 Out of Scope

Several real goodput drains are not modeled in this framework:

  • SLO-aware scheduling — admission control, request prioritization by deadline, preemption of low-priority requests. Production stacks ([SARATHI], [DYNAMO]) implement these to recover goodput when the offered load exceeds the static feasibility region. Modeling them requires queue-theoretic or simulation-based analysis.
  • Speculative decoding rejection — speculative-decoding pipelines emit tokens at higher peak rate but pay a rejection probability that affects effective TPOT. The roofline model captures the per-step time of speculative kernels but not the rejection-rate-driven goodput penalty.
  • Preemption-driven recompute — when the scheduler evicts a long-running request to admit a higher-priority one, the evicted request’s KV cache must be regenerated on resumption (kv.md §4.3). This is a real goodput cost and is not in our analytical model.
  • Cancellation effects — users abandoning long-running responses produce wasted compute that does not count toward goodput. The fraction is workload-specific and not modeled.

These omissions are intentional: each is a load-dependent or scheduler-dependent effect that lies outside the scope of a static roofline-based feasibility analysis. The bounds derived in §2–§4 are correct upper bounds on goodput under ideal scheduling; production deployments achieve some fraction of those bounds depending on scheduler quality and workload characteristics. A reasonable rule of thumb (consistent with [DISAGG-PREFILL] and [ALPASERVE] reported numbers): a well-tuned production stack achieves 60–80% of the analytical goodput bound; a poorly tuned one can achieve well under 30%.

6. Workload-Specific SLO Targets

The bounds of §2–§5 are parametric in the SLO targets. This section maps representative workload classes to their typical SLO-target ranges and identifies which bound binds in each class. The targets below are operational defaults observed across published serving benchmarks ([DISAGG-PREFILL], [VLLM], [DYNAMO]) and production deployment guides; specific deployments tune these to their own user-experience requirements.

6.1 Conversational Chat

Profile. Interactive multi-turn dialogue; user reads streaming output in real time; response lengths typically 50–300 tokens; prompt lengths 50–2000 tokens.

Typical SLOs. TTFTSLO​∈[200,500]ms at p95; TPOTSLO​∈[50,100]ms at p95 (10–20 tokens/s streaming).

Binding constraint. Both SLOs are typically loose enough that the binding constraint is neither — the deployment runs at the Zone-2 knee, and HBM capacity (KV-cache footprint at moderate B) is the binding constraint instead. The SLOs serve to eliminate shapes whose floor is above the TPOT bound (the §2.2 floor check) and whose prefill does not fit the TTFT budget (§3.1), but within the surviving shapes the goodput optimum is primarily HBM-driven. Production frameworks default to TP∈[4,8] and PP∈[1,4] for this class, with disaggregation rarely worthwhile since both phases have moderate latency budgets.

6.2 Agentic / Tool-Use

Profile. LLM-driven agents calling external tools, generating structured output (JSON, code), looping with intermediate verification; each LLM invocation is part of a larger pipeline whose user-perceived latency is the sum across many invocations. Response lengths often short (10–100 tokens, structured); prompt lengths often very long (5000–32000 tokens, including tool-output history).

Typical SLOs. TTFTSLO​∈[100,300]ms at p95 (tighter than chat — every invocation pays it); TPOTSLO​∈[30,50]ms at p95 (tighter than chat — short responses amplify per-token overhead). Long prompts make the TTFT side particularly tight.

Binding constraint. TTFTSLO​ is the dominant pressure. The combination of long prompts and tight TTFT targets demands wide tensor parallelism for prefill (§3.1); chunked prefill (§3.2) is essentially mandatory to keep long prompts from stalling decode. Disaggregation [DISAGG-PREFILL] is often worthwhile because the long-prompt-short-response asymmetry drives different optimal partitions for the two phases. The Zone-1 floor check (§2.2) typically rules out under-sharded shapes since long prompts inflate the per-token KV traffic, lowering B⋆ and the achievable B.

6.3 Batch / Offline Inference

Profile. Background processing — corpus summarization, document classification, large-scale evaluation, synthetic-data generation. No interactive user; the user-observable metric is end-to-end completion time of the entire job, not per-request latency.

Typical SLOs. TTFTSLO​→∞ (no per-request constraint); TPOTSLO​→∞. Practically: very loose targets at p50 to keep the worst-case throughput bounded (TPOTSLO​∈[500,2000]ms), but no tail constraint.

Binding constraint. Goodput maximization without SLO bounds reduces to throughput maximization. The optimal operating point is well into Zone 3 of the roofline (companion end-to-end derivation, §6.2), with B limited only by HBM capacity. Aggressive sharding is feasible since neither SLO bound binds, and deep PP earns its place here as a way to hold a larger batch in memory. The framework’s partition sweep without SLO filters (and the notebooks/pareto_basic.ipynb results) directly target this regime; the bounds derived in §2–§4 collapse to vacuous when both SLOs are infinite, recovering the throughput-only optimum.
